q-probability.whatItIs: P(event) = favourable ÷ total, with the counting done by combinations. At Clerk level it is almost always a bag of coloured balls, a pack of cards, or dice.
q-probability.coreMethod:
1. Write the TOTAL first: total = nCr where n is all the items and r is how many are drawn. This is the denominator for the whole question — compute it once and box it.
2. Write the FAVOURABLE count using the same combination logic, respecting the stated condition.
3. Divide and reduce. Bank answers are always clean fractions.
4. 'At least one' → 1 − P(none). Never enumerate cases.
5. 'Either A or B' when mutually exclusive → add. 'A and B' when independent → multiply. If they are not mutually exclusive, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B).
6. Two-colour draws: from 5 red and 7 blue, P(both red on a draw of 2) = 5C2 ÷ 12C2 = 10/66 = 5/33.
7. Standard reference numbers on instant recall:
   • A pack of 52: 26 red, 26 black, 13 per suit, 4 aces, 12 face cards, 4 of each rank
   • Two dice: 36 outcomes; P(sum = 7) = 6/36 = 1/6; P(doubles) = 6/36 = 1/6
   • n coins → 2ⁿ outcomes
8. WITHOUT replacement the denominator shrinks with each draw, so multiply sequential probabilities. WITH replacement the denominator is constant.
tricks: Compute the denominator once and reuse it — bank probability questions usually arrive in linked pairs sharing the same bag.
'At least one' = 1 − P(none) turns a three-case sum into a single subtraction. This is the highest-value single habit in the topic.
Reduce before you multiply: take 10/66 to 5/33 before it enters any further computation.
'One ball of each colour' from three colours is a plain product (5 × 7 × 3), not a sum of combinations.
Card denominators are almost always 52C1 = 52, 52C2 = 1326 or 52C3 = 22100. Recognising 1326 saves computing 52×51/2 every time.
Sanity check against the options: if every option exceeds 1/2 and your answer is below 1/2, you have computed the complement. Flip it rather than restarting.
traps: With versus without replacement. The paper states it in a single word and it changes the denominator of every subsequent draw.
'At least two' computed as 'exactly two' — the same under-count trap as in permutation and combination.
'Two cards are drawn' defaults to WITHOUT replacement unless the stem says otherwise. Assuming replacement is a silent, systematic error.
Using permutations for the favourable count while using combinations for the total (or the reverse). The two must be counted the same way — the ordering convention must match top and bottom.
Adding probabilities of events that are NOT mutually exclusive without subtracting the overlap. 'A king or a heart' has an overlap of one card.
Careless fraction reduction: 10/66 reduces to 5/33, not to 1/6.6. Any non-integer denominator means you have made an error.

q-calc.whatItIs: The mechanical layer beneath every other quantitative topic: multiplication and division shortcuts, squares and cubes, square and cube roots, fraction-to-percentage conversion, order of operations, and controlled approximation. In the paper it surfaces directly as the Simplification and Approximation set — a run of 'find the value of ?' lines that carry no concept at all and are pure calculation speed. Indirectly it decides your score everywhere else: a data interpretation set, a percentage problem and a partnership question all bottom out in the same arithmetic, so a slow calculation layer taxes every question you attempt. This is a motor-skill topic. You do not understand it and move on; you drill it until the answer arrives without conscious steps.
q-calc.coreMethod:
1. BUILD THE THREE REFERENCE TABLES AND OVER-LEARN THEM. Multiplication tables to 25. Squares to 40. Cubes to 20. These are not optional — every shortcut below assumes instant retrieval, and a shortcut that requires you to work out 17 squared is not a shortcut. Write each table daily for the first two weeks until you can produce any entry in under a second.

2. GET ORDER OF OPERATIONS EXACTLY RIGHT, AND KNOW WHEN IT ACTUALLY MATTERS. In Indian exam convention 'of' behaves as a bracketed multiplication: rewrite 'a of b' as (a x b) before doing anything else, then evaluate division and multiplication left to right, then addition and subtraction. The crucial and usually mistaught point is that this rewriting only CHANGES the answer when the word 'of' appears to the RIGHT of a division sign. Two checks. Case one, no divergence: 1/3 of 90 / 5 x 2. Doing 'of' first gives 30 / 5 x 2 = 12; going plain left to right gives (1/3 x 90) / 5 x 2 = 30 / 5 x 2 = 12. Identical, because 'of' was already leftmost — there was nothing to decide. Case two, genuine divergence: 36 / 3 of 4. Rewriting gives 36 / (3 x 4) = 36 / 12 = 3; strict left to right gives (36 / 3) x 4 = 12 x 4 = 48. Exam convention gives 3. So your working rule is: scan the line once for a division sign that has an 'of' anywhere to its right. If there is none, ignore the rule entirely and go left to right. If there is one, bracket that 'of' first.

3. MEMORISE THE PERCENT-FRACTION TABLE IN BOTH DIRECTIONS. 1/2 = 50%, 1/3 = 33 1/3%, 1/4 = 25%, 1/5 = 20%, 1/6 = 16 2/3%, 1/7 = 14 2/7%, 1/8 = 12.5%, 1/9 = 11 1/9%, 1/10 = 10%, 1/11 = 9 1/11%, 1/12 = 8 1/3%, 1/15 = 6 2/3%, 1/16 = 6.25%, 1/20 = 5%, 1/24 = 4 1/6%, 1/25 = 4%. Then use it in the fraction direction, which is where the time is saved: 62.5% of 848 is 5/8 of 848, and 848/8 = 106, so the answer is 530. Doing that as a decimal multiplication takes four times as long.

4. USE BASE-100 MULTIPLICATION FOR ANY TWO NUMBERS WITHIN ABOUT 12 OF 100. Write each number's difference from 100. Cross-add one number to the other's difference for the left part; multiply the two differences for the right part, written as two digits. Below 100: 94 x 96 — differences are -6 and -4, so 94 - 4 = 90 and 6 x 4 = 24, giving 9024. Above 100: 106 x 108 — differences +6 and +8, so 106 + 8 = 114 and 6 x 8 = 48, giving 11448. Both take about four seconds against roughly fifteen for long multiplication.

5. KEEP FOUR SMALL MULTIPLIERS AS REFLEXES. Times 11: split the digits and insert their sum, carrying if needed — 43 x 11 = 4|7|3 = 473, and 78 x 11 = 7|15|8 which carries to 858. Times 5: halve then move the decimal one place — 386 x 5 = 193 x 10 = 1930. Times 15: add half of ten times the number — 46 x 15 = 460 + 230 = 690. Squaring anything ending in 5: multiply the leading part by the next integer and append 25 — 65 squared is 6 x 7 = 42, then 25, giving 4225. Dividing by 5, 25 or 125 is the same idea reversed: multiply by 2, 4 or 8 and shift the decimal, so 385 / 5 = 770 / 10 = 77.

6. EXTRACT ROOTS BY LAST DIGIT PLUS RANGE. Square roots of perfect squares: the last digit of the number fixes the last digit of the root (a number ending in 9 has a root ending in 3 or 7; ending in 6 means 4 or 6; ending in 1 means 1 or 9; ending in 5 means 5; ending in 4 means 2 or 8). Then bracket the root between two multiples of ten. For 4489: last digit 9 so the root ends in 3 or 7; 4489 lies between 3600 and 4900 so the root is in the sixties; 65 squared is 4225 which is smaller, so the root is above 65, giving 67. Cube roots are easier because the last digit is unique: strip the last three digits, use the remaining part to fix the tens digit, and read the last digit off directly. For 12167: last digit 7 means the root ends in 3; the remaining 12 sits between 2 cubed and 3 cubed, so the tens digit is 2; the answer is 23.

7. HANDLE THE FIVE POSITIONS THE '?' CAN OCCUPY. Alone on one side — evaluate the other side and you are done. Inside a sum or difference — evaluate both known parts, then subtract. As a percentage — '? % of 750 = 45% of 200' gives 90 = 7.5 x ?, so ? = 12. Under a root or as a power — isolate, then undo the operation: '? squared + 15 squared = 17 squared' gives ? squared = 289 - 225 = 64, so ? = 8; 'root of ? + 17 = 36' gives root of ? = 19, so ? = 361; '? cubed = 5832' gives ? = 18. Inside a fraction — cross-multiply once and do not simplify twice.

8. SEPARATE APPROXIMATION FROM EXACT WORK BEFORE THE FIRST STROKE. If the line uses an approximation sign, round every term to a convenient anchor and stop: 24.97% of 1599.8 + 39.98% of 749.9 becomes a quarter of 1600 plus two-fifths of 750, which is 400 + 300 = 700. If the line uses an equals sign, you must be exact. Deciding this after you have started is what costs twenty seconds a question.

9. BOUND YOUR ROUNDING DELIBERATELY. When approximating, round one term up and the other down and note that your answer now sits between two computable values. This gives a genuine interval rather than a hope, and if two options fall inside your interval it tells you honestly that you rounded too coarsely and must redo one term more finely. It is a check, not a shortcut past the arithmetic.

10. FIX A PAPER LAYOUT AND NEVER VARY IT. Write the '?' isolated on its own line before computing anything. Keep one vertical column per question on the rough sheet. Do not compute across the page. Most calculation errors in this topic are transcription errors, not arithmetic errors, and layout is the only thing that removes them.

11. DRILL DAILY WITH A CLOCK, NOT WITH A TARGET SCORE. Twenty mixed simplification and approximation questions against a timer at the start of every quantitative session. Record time and accuracy separately. Speed without accuracy is worth negative marks here; accuracy without speed loses you the questions you never reach.
tricks: Read percentages as fractions in one direction only — towards the fraction. 37.5% of 640 becomes 3/8 of 640 = 240 in about three seconds; the same product done as 0.375 x 640 takes fifteen. Over a 13-question simplification block this single habit is worth more than two minutes.

Base-100 multiplication for any pair within roughly 12 of 100 turns a fifteen-second long multiplication into a four-second cross-add. The same method works around a base of 50 or 1000 once the base-100 version is automatic.

Last-digit extraction for roots removes the trial-and-error entirely. Cube roots of perfect cubes are the strongest case because every last digit maps to exactly one root digit, so a four- or five-digit cube root becomes a two-second read rather than a search.

Convert every division by 5, 25 or 125 into a multiplication by 2, 4 or 8 with a decimal shift. Division is the slowest operation on paper and the most error-prone; this removes it from a large share of lines at no cost.

Scan the whole line before writing anything, looking for exactly two things: whether the sign is 'approximately equal to' or 'equals', and whether any division sign has an 'of' to its right. Those two checks take three seconds and determine your entire method for the question. Starting to compute before making them is what produces a correct calculation of the wrong expression.
traps: Applying the 'of binds first' rule where it changes nothing, and missing it where it matters. In 1/3 of 90 / 5 x 2 both readings give 12, so the rule is irrelevant and thinking about it wastes time. In 84 / 7 of 2 the readings genuinely diverge: bracketing gives 84 / (7 x 2) = 6, while plain left to right gives (84 / 7) x 2 = 24. Divergence happens only when an 'of' sits to the right of a division sign — check for that specific shape, not for the presence of the word.

Treating an approximation line as exact, or an exact line as approximate. If the stem uses the approximation sign the options are spread far apart and exact work is wasted; if it uses equals and the options are two apart, rounding 8.98% to 9% will put you between two options and cost the question. The sign at the head of the line is the instruction.

Decimal-place slip on small percentages. 0.5% of 800 is 4, not 40 — aspirants read 0.5% as 5% under time pressure. The same slip appears with 0.25% and 1.5%. Convert to a fraction of 100 explicitly rather than moving a decimal point by eye.

Sign lost through a nested bracket. 45 - (12 - 8 x 2) resolves as 45 - (12 - 16) = 45 - (-4) = 49, not 41. The inner multiplication makes the bracket negative and the outer minus then adds. Aspirants who compute the bracket as a positive 4 land on a number that is also among the options.

Mixed fractions divided only in part. 5 3/4 divided by 1/4 requires converting to 23/4 first, giving 23/4 x 4 = 23. Dividing only the fractional part gives 5 3/16, which looks like a plausible answer and is wrong. Convert every mixed fraction to an improper fraction before any operation touches it.

Distributing a root or a square over a sum. The square root of (9 + 16) is 5, not 3 + 4 = 7. The same error appears as (a + b) squared computed as a squared plus b squared. Both wrong values are routinely planted among the five options because they are the natural output of the mistake.
q-calc.timeTarget: 15–25 seconds per simplification or approximation question at exam speed. The 13-question block in Prelims Numerical Ability should close in 4.5 to 5.5 minutes, leaving roughly 14 of the 20 sectional minutes for the remaining 22 questions. In Mains the same lines run slightly heavier — budget 20–30 seconds each. During practice, expect 45 seconds a question in week one and drive it down over six weeks; the target is what a trained aspirant achieves, not what a beginner should expect on day one.
q-calc.masteryCheck: Set a six-minute timer and attempt 20 mixed questions — 12 exact simplifications and 8 approximations, drawn from a source you have not seen. Pass is 18 correct with at most one attempted-and-wrong, because a wrong attempt costs 0.25 against leaving it blank and 1.25 against getting it right, so an aggressive-and-inaccurate run is worse than a slower clean one. Separately, and away from any question paper, write the squares to 40, the cubes to 20 and the full percent-fraction table from memory in under four minutes with no errors. You own the topic when you clear 18 out of 20 inside five minutes on three consecutive attempts spread over a week, and when the tables come out clean without hesitation.
questionPatterns: Straight simplification with '?' isolated: '(root of 1296 / 4) x 15 = ?' — the root is 36, 36/4 = 9, 9 x 15 = 135. Five options clustered near 135 with the common slips planted.
Percentage combination: '15% of 480 + 24% of 250 = ?' — 72 + 60 = 132. Options will include 122 and 142, which are what a single arithmetic slip produces.

'?' under a root or as a power: '? squared + 15 squared = 17 squared' gives ? squared = 289 - 225 = 64 so ? = 8; 'root of ? + 17 = 36' gives ? = 361; '? cubed = 5832' gives ? = 18. All three resolve to clean integers, which is the standard for this question type — if your working produces a non-integer you have misread the expression.
'?' as the percentage: '? % of 750 = 45% of 200' — the right side is 90, so 7.5 x ? = 90 and ? = 12.

Approximation: '24.97% of 1599.8 + 39.98% of 749.9 = approximately ?' — round to a quarter of 1600 plus two-fifths of 750 = 400 + 300 = 700. Options are spread 50 or more apart, which is the signal that rounding is intended.

Order-of-operations line with a genuine 'of' after a division: '36 / 3 of 4 + 17 = ?' — bracket the 'of' first, giving 36/12 = 3, then 3 + 17 = 20. The plain left-to-right reading gives 48 + 17 = 65, which will be among the five options.
Mixed-fraction line: '5 3/4 / 1/4 - 6 = ?' — convert to 23/4, multiply by 4 to get 23, then subtract 6 for 17.

q-calc.blockPlan: This is warm-up, not a topic with a finish date. Week 1: one dedicated 60-minute quant block to build the three reference tables and the percent-fraction card, plus the order-of-operations rule with both the divergent and non-divergent cases written out. Then, permanently: the first 10 minutes of EVERY quantitative session, every day, is a timed 20-question calculation drill — 6 minutes on the clock, 4 minutes reviewing which questions were slow and why. Do not do this at the end of a session when you are tired; the point is that it runs when you are fresh, because you are training a reflex, not learning a concept. Add one 30-minute session per week for the first four weeks on the shortcut set specifically — base-100, times-11, roots by last digit — practising each in isolation until it stops requiring thought. Expect visible speed gains by the end of week two and something close to exam pace by week six; the daily 10 minutes then continues untouched all the way to December because the reflex decays within about a week of stopping.

They are also the fastest-resolving questions in the section, so this block is where the time for data interpretation and word problems has to be earned. In Mains the direct count drops to roughly 4 of 40, but the indirect exposure is total: every DI set, percentage, ratio, average and interest question resolves through the same arithmetic, so calculation speed sets a ceiling on the whole quantitative score in both papers. Sequence it first, before any conceptual quant topic, and keep it running daily rather than closing it.

q-simpl-2.whatItIs: Long numeric expressions where the five options are spaced widely enough that you are meant to round rather than compute exactly — together with the deliberately tight-spaced variants where the rounding must be controlled or abandoned. In Prelims it is a block of fast marks that funds the rest of the section. In Mains it is a handful of direct questions plus the engine inside every DI computation you make.
q-simpl-2.coreMethod:
1. READ THE FIVE OPTIONS BEFORE YOU READ THE EXPRESSION. The gap between the two closest options is your rounding licence. Options of 180 / 195 / 210 / 225 / 240 sit about 7% apart and permit aggressive rounding. Options of 193 / 195 / 197 / 199 / 201 sit about 1% apart, which means you round only terms that are genuinely within about 0.2% and compute the rest. This step comes first because you cannot choose a rounding strategy you have not been licensed for.
2. ROUND EVERY TERM TO ITS NEAREST FRIENDLY ANCHOR AND WRITE THE ROUNDED EXPRESSION ON ONE LINE before evaluating anything: 19.98 to 20, 24.97 to 25, 33.29 to 33.33 (which is 1/3), 12.49 to 12.5 (which is 1/8), 624.99 to 625, 1439.87 to 1440, 799.87 to 800.
3. MARK THE DIRECTION OF EACH ROUNDING with a small plus or minus. If you rounded the numerator up and the denominator down, your result is too large. When your computed value falls between two options, that mark tells you which side to take. This is a control on your own arithmetic — it never replaces computing, and you never pick an option without a value in hand.
4. PERCENTAGES BECOME FRACTIONS IMMEDIATELY. 24.98% of 799.87 is (1/4) x 800 = 200; 12.51% of 1599.6 is (1/8) x 1600 = 200; the sum is 400.
5. ROOTS: square-root 624.99 is square-root 625 = 25; cube-root 3374.8 is cube-root 3375 = 15. If the number under the root is not near a perfect power, bracket it — 3480 lies between 58 squared (3364) and 59 squared (3481), so it is 59 to the nearest integer.
6. DIVIDE BEFORE YOU MULTIPLY WHEN IT CANCELS. 1439.87 divided by 11.98 times 4.02 becomes 1440/12 = 120, then times 4 = 480. Cancelling first keeps every intermediate value under three digits.
7. DIFFERENCE OF SQUARES, NEVER TWO SQUARINGS. (17.94) squared minus (12.02) squared becomes (18 - 12)(18 + 12) = 6 x 30 = 180.
8. 'OF' CHAINS RUN LEFT TO RIGHT WITH CANCELLATION: seven-eighths of 2399.8 is 2400 x 7/8 = 2100.
9. WRITE ONLY THE RUNNING VALUE DOWN THE PAGE, one number per line. Never rewrite the whole expression — rewriting is where transcription errors enter, and at 15 seconds a question you have no budget for a second reading.
10. IF AFTER 25 SECONDS YOU HAVE NO CLEAN ANCHOR, MOVE ON. This block exists to be fast. A slow approximation question has already cost more than it is worth, and there are eleven more of them in the paper.
tricks: The 1/n table to 1/16 memorised as percentages: 1/6 = 16.67%, 1/7 = 14.29%, 1/8 = 12.5%, 1/9 = 11.11%, 1/11 = 9.09%, 1/12 = 8.33%, 1/13 = 7.69%, 1/14 = 7.14%, 1/16 = 6.25%. Most 'percent of' terms in this block are disguised versions of these and resolve on sight rather than by multiplication.
Squares to 30 and cubes to 15 held cold, so that any square or root term is recognised rather than computed. This alone turns a 25-second root question into an 8-second one.

When a term is genuinely awkward, anchor it BOTH ways — to the round number above and to the one below — evaluate both, and see which single option lies between them. Two fast bounds beat one slow exact value, and the bounds are a proof rather than a guess.
Multiplying by 5, 25, 50 or 125: use 10/2, 100/4, 100/2 and 1000/8. 348 x 25 = 34800/4 = 8700, done in one division.
Split awkward percentage rates additively: 18% of 450 = 10% (45) + 5% (22.5) + 3% (13.5) = 81. Faster than long multiplication and each part is self-checking.

Read the operator sequence once before you round anything. A single division you took as a multiplication makes every rounding decision that follows irrelevant, and it costs you the question with a penalty attached.
traps: Rounding numerator and denominator in the SAME direction and assuming the errors cancel. They do not cancel — same-direction roundings compound. Only opposite-direction roundings partly offset, which is exactly why step 3 asks you to mark the direction.

Option sets deliberately spaced 1-2% apart to punish aggressive rounding. Rounding 2449 up to 2500 is a 2.08% error, which on a 1% option spread guarantees the wrong pick — and that wrong pick is a printed option, so it costs a quarter mark on top.
Reading 33.33% as one-third when the expression actually says 3.33% (one-thirtieth) or 333.3%. The decimal point is the entire question and the three corresponding answers are all in the option list.

Percentage versus percentage point in stems where the base is itself a percentage: 'the rate increased by 15%' and 'the rate increased by 15 percentage points' are different operations with different answers.

BODMAS abandoned under time pressure: 12 + 8 x 5 is 52, not 100. Approximation expressions are written with mixed operators precisely to catch left-to-right evaluation, and the left-to-right value is always an option.

Rounding a term that the option spread does not permit you to round, because you never looked at the options. This is step 1 being skipped, and it is the most common single cause of misses in an otherwise well-drilled candidate.

q-numsys.whatItIs: Divisibility, unit digits, remainders, and the HCF/LCM word problems (bells tolling together, greatest number that divides leaving remainders, least number leaving a common remainder). Low direct weight, but the LCM habit powers Time-and-Work and Pipes.
q-numsys.coreMethod:
1. HCF by Euclid's division: divide the larger by the smaller, then the divisor by the remainder, repeat until remainder 0. HCF(1001, 910): 1001 = 910x1 + 91; 910 = 91x10 + 0 -> HCF = 91.
2. LCM by prime powers: take the highest power of each prime present. LCM(12,18,20) = 2^2 x 3^2 x 5 = 180. For two numbers only, LCM = product / HCF.
3. MASTER IDENTITY: Product of two numbers = HCF x LCM. Also, the two numbers are ALWAYS H x a and H x b where H is the HCF and a, b are coprime. 'HCF is 12, LCM is 144, one number is 36 — find the other': other = 12x144/36 = 48.
4. THE FIVE WORD-PROBLEM FORMS (learn these as templates, they are the whole topic):
   a. Greatest number that divides x, y, z leaving remainders a, b, c -> HCF(x-a, y-b, z-c).
   b. Greatest number that divides x, y, z leaving the SAME (unknown) remainder -> HCF of the pairwise differences: HCF(y-x, z-y, z-x).
   c. Least number which when divided by a, b, c leaves the same remainder r -> LCM(a,b,c) + r.
   d. Least number which when divided by a, b, c leaves remainders p, q, r where (a-p) = (b-q) = (c-r) = k -> LCM(a,b,c) - k.
   e. Bells/lights/traffic signals ringing together -> LCM of the intervals. Number of times in T seconds INCLUDING the start = T/LCM + 1.
5. FRACTIONS: HCF of fractions = HCF(numerators)/LCM(denominators). LCM of fractions = LCM(numerators)/HCF(denominators).
6. UNIT DIGIT via cyclicity 4: divide the power by 4, use the remainder; remainder 0 means use the 4th term. Cycles: 2 -> (2,4,8,6); 3 -> (3,9,7,1); 7 -> (7,9,3,1); 8 -> (8,4,2,6); 4 -> (4,6); 9 -> (9,1); 0,1,5,6 -> themselves. Unit digit of 7^83: 83 = 4x20+3 -> third term of (7,9,3,1) -> 3.
7. DIVISIBILITY RULES worth knowing: by 4 (last two digits), 8 (last three), 3 and 9 (digit sum), 11 (alternating digit sum divisible by 11), 7 (double the last digit and subtract from the rest, repeat), 6 (2 and 3 together).
8. REMAINDER SHORTCUT: to find the remainder of a product, take remainders first and multiply them. Remainder of (17 x 23) / 5 = (2 x 3)/5 -> 6/5 -> 1.
tricks: Product = HCF x LCM turns almost every two-number question into one division. Also use it to sanity-check: HCF must divide LCM exactly — if it doesn't, you've misread the question.
For 'same remainder, remainder unknown', go straight to the DIFFERENCES. Beginners waste 60 seconds trying to guess the remainder.

Bells: the answer to 'how many times in 1 hour' is 3600/LCM + 1, and the +1 (the initial simultaneous ring) is what the options are testing. Also check whether the LCM is in seconds while the period is in minutes.
Build LCMs of small numbers by prime powers, not by long division ladders — LCM(8,12,15,20) = 2^3 x 3 x 5 = 120 takes four seconds.
Unit digit of any number ending in 5 or 6 raised to any power is 5 or 6. Numbers ending in 0 give 0, in 1 give 1. That kills half the unit-digit questions instantly.
traps: Confusing template (a) with template (b): 'leaving remainders 3, 5, 7' is a different calculation from 'leaving the same remainder'.
Off-by-one on the bells problem — forgetting that they also rang together at the start.
Intervals given in seconds but the question asks 'in 2 hours' — convert before, not after.
Remainder larger than the divisor in your working, or an option where the remainder exceeds the divisor — that option is always wrong, eliminate it free.
HCF/LCM of fractions: swapping the two formulas. HCF uses HCF on top; LCM uses LCM on top. Say it aloud: 'the operation name goes on top'.

q-percentage.whatItIs: The spine of the entire Quant section. Profit-loss, interest, DI, mixture and data comparison are all percentage questions in costume. It tests whether you can move between a percentage, a fraction and a ratio without computing.
q-percentage.coreMethod:
1. NEVER MULTIPLY BY A DECIMAL. Convert to the table fraction and cancel. 62.5% of 288 = 5/8 x 288 = 180. 8.33% of 1560 = 1560/12 = 130.
2. 'A IS x% MORE/LESS THAN B' -> convert to a RATIO immediately. x% more, where x = 1/n as a fraction, gives A:B = (n+1):n. So: 25% (1/4) more -> 5:4. 20% (1/5) more -> 6:5. 33.33% (1/3) more -> 4:3. 16.67% (1/6) more -> 7:6. 12.5% (1/8) more -> 9:8. 11.11% (1/9) more -> 10:9. For 'less', flip: 20% less -> 4:5; 25% less -> 3:4.
3. THE REVERSE PAIR (memorise as pairs, this is the highest-yield single fact in the topic): if A is 1/n MORE than B, then B is 1/(n+1) LESS than A. So 25% more <-> 20% less; 33.33% more <-> 25% less; 20% more <-> 16.67% less; 12.5% more <-> 11.11% less; 100% more <-> 50% less. IBPS asks this both ways every year.
4. SUCCESSIVE CHANGE: net% = a + b + ab/100, signs included. +20% then -10% -> 20 - 10 - 200/100 = +8%. Or just multiply the fractions: 6/5 x 9/10 = 54/50 = +8%.
5. EQUAL UP-THEN-DOWN is always a LOSS of x^2/100 %. +20% then -20% -> 4% net loss. Never zero.
6. UNITARY, NOT ALGEBRA: 'if 15% of a number is 45, what is 40% of it?' -> 45/15 x 40 = 120. Do not find the number.
7. THE MARKS PATTERN: 'A scores 30% and fails by 40 marks; B scores 45% and gets 20 marks more than the pass mark.' The DIFFERENCE in percentages maps to the DIFFERENCE in marks: 15% = 60 marks -> total = 400. Pass mark = 120+40 = 160.
8. EXPENDITURE / CONSUMPTION: if price rises by x%, consumption must fall by x/(100+x) x 100 % to keep expenditure constant. Price up 25% (1/4) -> consumption down 1/5 = 20%. This is just the reverse-pair rule again.
9. TWO-STEP POPULATION/SALARY: P x (1 + a/100) x (1 - b/100). Use fraction multipliers (11/10, 6/5, 9/10, 4/5) so the numbers cancel against P.
10. ALWAYS UNDERLINE THE BASE. Write '% of WHAT' beside every percentage in the question before you compute anything.
tricks: The reverse-pair table (25% more = 20% less, 33.33% more = 25% less, 20% more = 16.67% less, 12.5% more = 11.11% less, 16.67% more = 14.28% less) converts a whole class of questions into a 3-second lookup.
x% of y = y% of x. 18% of 50 = 50% of 18 = 9. 64% of 25 = 25% of 64 = 16. Use whichever side is friendlier.
To increase by a table fraction, multiply directly: +37.5% is x11/8; +62.5% is x13/8; +12.5% is x9/8; +16.67% is x7/6. To decrease: -37.5% is x5/8; -16.67% is x5/6.
Equal-percentage up-then-down is ALWAYS x^2/100 loss. If an option says 'no change', it is wrong by construction.
In marks/pass-fail problems, subtract the two scenarios first — the unknown total drops out of a difference and you get the total in one division.
15% = 10% + 5% (halve the ten); 45% = 50% - 5%; 35% = 25% + 10%. Building percentages out of 10%, 5% and 1% chunks beats any multiplication.
traps: Percentage POINTS vs percent. A rise from 20% to 25% is 5 percentage points but a 25% increase. IBPS puts both 5 and 25 in the options.
Adding successive percentages: 20% then 20% is 44%, not 40%; 20% then -20% is -4%, not 0.
Base shifting mid-question: 'B is 20% less than A' does NOT mean 'A is 20% more than B'. It means A is 25% more than B.
'x% more than' vs 'x% of'. '60% more than 200' is 320; '60% of 200' is 120. Both appear as options.
In pass-fail problems, confusing the TOTAL marks with the PASSING marks — the question usually asks for one and the fast route gives you the other first.

q-ratio.whatItIs: Splitting a quantity into given parts, chaining two or three ratios that share a term, and handling a ratio that changes when a fixed number is added to or subtracted from both terms. Ratio is not really a chapter — it is the notation that partnership, mixture, ages, boats, time-and-work and most DI comparison questions are written in. Weak ratio handling does not show up as marks lost here; it shows up as slowness everywhere else.
q-ratio.coreMethod:
1. ONE VARIABLE, ALWAYS. The moment you read 'a : b = 3 : 5' write 3k and 5k on the rough sheet. Never two letters. Every Clerk-level ratio question then collapses to a single linear equation in k.
2. IF THE STEM GIVES A SUM OR A DIFFERENCE, DO NOT FORM AN EQUATION — DIVIDE. a:b = 5:8 with b - a = 24: the gap is 3 parts, so k = 8, giving 40 and 64. Same ratio with a + b = 91: 13 parts, k = 7, giving 35 and 56. Trigger words: 'their sum is', 'their difference is', 'exceeds by', 'is more than ... by'.
3. CHAIN TWO RATIOS BY SCALING THE SHARED TERM TO ITS LCM. A:B = 2:3 and B:C = 4:5. LCM(3,4) = 12, so A:B = 8:12 and B:C = 12:15, giving A:B:C = 8:12:15. Fewer multiplications than the cross-multiply rule and the numbers stay small.
4. CHAIN THREE THE SAME WAY, LEFT TO RIGHT. A:B = 2:3, B:C = 4:5, C:D = 6:7. First LCM(3,4) = 12 gives 8:12:15. Then LCM(15,6) = 30, so double the first block to 16:24:30 and write C:D as 30:35. Result A:B:C:D = 16:24:30:35. Check it back: 16:24 = 2:3, 24:30 = 4:5, 30:35 = 6:7.
5. RATIO CHANGED BY ADDING OR SUBTRACTING A FIXED NUMBER — write the new ratio as one equation and cross-multiply once. 'The ratio is 3:5; adding 4 to each makes it 5:7': (3k+4)/(5k+4) = 5/7 gives 21k + 28 = 25k + 20, so k = 2 and the numbers are 6 and 10. Verify: 10/14 = 5/7.
6. FRACTIONAL RELATIONS — set the LAST-mentioned quantity to 1, work backwards, clear denominators with the LCM. 'A gets two-thirds of what B gets; B gets one-quarter of what C gets': C = 1, B = 1/4, A = 1/6. Multiply by 12: A:B:C = 2:3:12.
7. DIVIDING A SUM. Share = (own parts / total parts) x sum. The DIFFERENCE of two shares comes in one step: (parts difference / total parts) x sum.
8. WEIGHTED OR DENOMINATION RATIOS — when the ratio counts ITEMS THAT HAVE DIFFERENT VALUES, first compute the value of one whole block. Coins of Rs 1, Rs 2 and Rs 5 in the ratio 3:4:5 by number: one block is worth 3(1) + 4(2) + 5(5) = Rs 36. Total Rs 540 means 15 blocks, so there are 60 two-rupee coins. Check: 45 + 120 + 375 = 540.
9. PROPORTION VOCABULARY — four one-line formulas, learn all four. a:b :: c:d means ad = bc. Mean proportional between a and b = sqrt(ab). Third proportional to a and b = b^2/a. Fourth proportional to a, b, c = bc/a. (Fourth proportional to 4, 9, 12 = 9x12/4 = 27; mean proportional between 8 and 32 = sqrt(256) = 16.)
10. BEFORE WRITING THE ANSWER, RE-READ THE LAST SIX WORDS OF THE STEM. Circle whether it wants the smaller, the larger, a ratio, a share, or k itself.
tricks: Sum-of-parts / difference-of-parts gives you k in a single division with no equation at all. Recognising the trigger words ('sum is', 'difference is', 'exceeds by') and dividing immediately saves roughly 15 seconds per question, and this family is a large slice of all direct ratio stems.
Ratio to percentage with no division: in 3:5 the parts are 3/8 and 5/8, which the fraction table reads off as 37.5% and 62.5%. Any 'what percent of the total' ratio stem becomes instant.

Scale-to-LCM chaining instead of cross-multiplying: A:B = 2:3 with B:C = 4:5 needs LCM(3,4) = 12, giving 8:12:15 directly. You write two numbers instead of six and the result is usually already in lowest terms.

Difference of two shares in one calculation: Rs 8400 split in 8:12:15 has 35 parts, so C - A = (7/35) x 8400 = Rs 1680. Computing both shares separately takes two divisions and a subtraction for the same answer.

Income : expenditure stems — savings is always the DIFFERENCE of the parts, so income = (income parts / savings parts) x savings. With 5:4 and savings Rs 6000, one part is 6000 and income is Rs 30,000 in one multiplication.

Direction sanity check (a check on your arithmetic, never a substitute for it): adding the same positive number to both terms always pulls a ratio TOWARDS 1:1, subtracting pushes it AWAY. 3:5 is 0.60; adding 4 to each gives 7:9 = 0.78, closer to 1. If your k makes the ratio move the wrong way you transposed the cross-multiplication — redo it, do not pick.
traps: Order reversal. The stem says 'the ratio of B to A' or asks for the SMALLER number while you solved for the larger. The reversed value is placed among the five options every single time.

Treating the shared term of two ratios as already equal. A:B = 2:3 with B:C = 4:5 read as A:B:C = 2:3:5 or 2:4:5. B is 3 in one statement and 4 in the other; you must scale to LCM(3,4) = 12 before combining. This is the most expensive single misreading in the topic.
Adding ratios. 2:3 'combined with' 3:4 is not 5:7. Ratios of different totals cannot be added — convert both to actual quantities first, then add the quantities.

Reading a ratio of COUNTS as a ratio of VALUES. 'Coins of Rs 1, 2 and 5 in the ratio 3:4:5' counts coins, so one block is worth Rs 36, not Rs 12. Dividing the total by 3+4+5 = 12 is the manufactured wrong answer and it is always an option.
The ratio is stated for a past or future situation ('five years ago their ages were in the ratio 4:5') while the question asks for a present value. Write the tense next to your k-expression.
Answering with k. You find k = 8 and mark 8 when the question wanted 5k = 40. The value of k is deliberately included in the options.

q-average.whatItIs: The arithmetic mean, and the small family of standard manipulations built on it: replacing a member of a group, adding one, correcting a wrongly recorded value, merging two groups of unequal size, tracking a group's average age across time, and the special case of average speed. In Clerk Prelims it appears as short standalone word problems; in Mains it appears both standalone and folded into data interpretation and mixture questions. The whole topic runs off a single identity — Sum equals Average times Count — and almost every question is solved faster by working with the change in the sum than by computing either total. The examinable difficulty is never the arithmetic; it is reading which of six situations the stem describes.
q-average.coreMethod:
1. CONVERT EVERY STEM TO SUMS IN THE FIRST FIVE SECONDS. Write Sum = Average x Count for each group mentioned before you do anything else. Averages cannot be added, subtracted or compared across groups of different sizes; sums can. Nearly every wrong answer in this topic comes from operating on averages that were never comparable.

2. USE THE DEVIATION METHOD FOR ANY SET OF CLOSE NUMBERS. Pick a convenient assumed mean, add up the deviations, divide by the count and add back. For 246, 251, 249, 254, 250, assume 250: the deviations are -4, +1, -1, +4, 0, which sum to zero, so the average is 250. You never touch a four-digit total. This is the difference between eight seconds and forty.

3. KNOW THE AP SHORTCUTS COLD. For any set of numbers in arithmetic progression, including consecutive integers, the average is (first + last)/2 — and for an odd count it is simply the middle term. The average of the first n natural numbers is (n+1)/2. The average of the first n odd numbers is n. The average of the first n even numbers is n+1. Check the last two: the first five odd numbers are 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 with average 5, which equals n; the first five even numbers are 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 with average 6, which equals n+1.

4. REPLACEMENT — THE COUNT DOES NOT CHANGE. When a new member replaces an existing one, the sum changes by exactly (new value - old value), so new = old + n x (change in average). Worked: the average weight of 8 people rises by 2.5 kg when a new person replaces one weighing 65 kg. New person = 65 + 8 x 2.5 = 85 kg.

5. INCLUSION — THE COUNT GOES UP BY ONE, AND THE FORMULA IS DIFFERENT. When an extra member joins n existing members, the new member equals the NEW average plus n times the change in average. Worked: 30 students average 15 years; including the teacher raises the average by 1, so the teacher is 16 + 30 x 1 = 46. Verify by sums: 31 x 16 = 496, minus 30 x 15 = 450, gives 46. Confusing this with the replacement rule in step 4 is the single most expensive error in the topic.

6. CORRECTION OF A WRONG ENTRY. The change in average is (correct value - wrong value) divided by n. Worked: the average of 10 numbers was computed as 15; one number had been read as 26 instead of 62. The sum was understated by 36, so the average was understated by 3.6, and the correct average is 18.6.

7. MERGING GROUPS — WEIGHTED AVERAGE, NEVER THE MEAN OF THE MEANS. Combined average = (sum of group sums) / (sum of counts). Worked: 30 students averaging 60 and 20 students averaging 70 give (1800 + 1400)/50 = 64, not 65.

8. SPLIT A GROUP WITH ALLIGATION. When a combined average is known along with the two sub-group averages, the ratio of the two counts is found by taking the differences cross-wise: count of high group : count of low group = (overall - low) : (high - overall). Worked: 20 employees average Rs 8,000; managers average Rs 20,000 and the rest Rs 5,000. Ratio of managers to others = (8000 - 5000) : (20000 - 8000) = 3000 : 12000 = 1 : 4, so out of 20 there are 4 managers and 16 others. Verify: 4 x 20000 + 16 x 5000 = 80,000 + 80,000 = 1,60,000, and 1,60,000 / 20 = 8,000. Correct.

9. AGES ACROSS TIME — EVERYONE AGES, SO THE SUM RISES BY n TIMES t. This is the step aspirants get wrong by adding only t. Worked: four years ago the average age of a family of 4 was 24 years. A baby is born, and today the average age of all 5 members is again 24 years. Find the baby's age. Four years ago the sum was 4 x 24 = 96. Today those same four members total 96 + (4 x 4) = 112. Today all five total 5 x 24 = 120. The baby is 120 - 112 = 8 years old. Check the whole thing forwards: the four members average 112/4 = 28 today, and (112 + 8)/5 = 24. Consistent.

10. AVERAGE SPEED IS NOT AN ARITHMETIC MEAN WHEN THE DISTANCES ARE EQUAL. For equal distances at speeds a and b, average speed = 2ab/(a+b). At 40 km/h out and 60 km/h back, the average is 2 x 40 x 60 / 100 = 48 km/h, not 50. When the TIMES are equal instead of the distances, the arithmetic mean is correct — read which one the stem fixes.

11. THE INNINGS PATTERN. A batsman in his 17th innings scores 85 and thereby raises his average by 3. Let the average after the 17th be x. Then 17x = 16(x - 3) + 85, so 17x = 16x + 37 and x = 37. The general shape: total after = total before + this score, with the 'before' average written as (x - increase).

12. DRILL BY CLASSIFICATION BEFORE CALCULATION. Take 20 mixed average questions and, without solving any of them, write only which of the six situations each one is — replacement, inclusion, correction, merge, split, or ages-across-time. Two minutes for all twenty. Misclassification, not arithmetic, is what loses this topic.
tricks: Work with the change in the sum, never the sums themselves. In a replacement question the entire answer is old value plus n times the change in average — one multiplication and one addition. Computing both totals to subtract them takes four times as long and introduces two chances to slip.

Use the assumed-mean deviation method whenever the numbers cluster. Choosing a mean in the middle of the cluster turns four-digit addition into single-digit addition, and the deviations often cancel to zero or something trivially small.

For any arithmetic progression, read the average straight off as (first + last)/2 — or as the middle term when the count is odd. Questions asking for the average of 20 consecutive numbers or the first 50 natural numbers become one-step reads rather than summations.

Alligation gives the ratio of the two sub-group counts in one cross-subtraction, which is far quicker than setting up and solving 20000m + 5000(20 - m) = 160000. It also gives you a free consistency check: the total headcount must be a whole-number multiple of the ratio sum, so if it is not, you have paired the differences the wrong way round.

For equal-distance average speed, recognise the shape and apply 2ab/(a+b) directly. Two speeds and one journey out and back is the signal. Deriving it from distance-over-time each time costs twenty seconds you will need elsewhere.
traps: Inclusion treated as replacement. 'A teacher is included' takes the count from n to n+1 and uses new member = new average + n x (change). 'A person is replaced' keeps the count at n and uses new = old + n x (change). The two stems read almost identically and the two formulas give different numbers; identify which one the verb describes before touching the arithmetic.

Ages across time with only t added instead of n times t. If a group of 5 was averaging 20 four years ago, their total today is not 100 + 4 — it is 100 + (5 x 4) = 120, because every one of the five members aged four years. This is the error that produces impossible answers like a negative or zero age, and an impossible answer is itself the signal that you added t once.

Average speed taken as the arithmetic mean over equal distances. 40 and 60 give 48, not 50. The 50 is always among the options because it is what the mistake produces. The arithmetic mean is only correct when the two speeds are held for equal TIMES, which is a different stem.

'Increases by' versus 'increases to'. 'The average increases by 2' means the change is 2; 'the average increases to 2' would mean the new average is 2. Similarly 'is 3 more than' describes a difference while 'becomes 3 times' describes a ratio. One preposition changes the equation entirely.

Alligation differences paired the wrong way round. The count of the HIGH-average group pairs with (overall - low), and the count of the LOW group pairs with (high - overall). Crossing them gives the reciprocal ratio, which usually produces a non-integer headcount — treat a fractional number of people as proof you inverted the ratio, and re-pair rather than rounding.

Merged average taken as the mean of the two averages. Groups of 30 at 60 and 20 at 70 give 64, not 65. The mean of the means is only right when the two groups are the same size, and 65 will be an option every time.

q-ages.whatItIs: Two or three people whose ages are given as a ratio now and a different ratio at some other time. It is a one-variable linear equation dressed up in tense changes, and it appears in almost every Clerk Prelims paper.
q-ages.coreMethod:
1. SET AGES AS RATIO PARTS, not letters. Ratio 4:5 now -> present ages are 4x and 5x. Only use separate letters if no ratio is given.
2. APPLY THE TENSE SHIFT TO EVERY PERSON. 'Five years ago' subtracts 5 from ALL of them; 'after 8 years' adds 8 to ALL of them. Write the shifted ages in a second row underneath before forming the equation.
3. FORM ONE EQUATION AND CROSS-MULTIPLY. Present 3:4, after 6 years 5:6 -> (3x+6)/(4x+6) = 5/6 -> 18x + 36 = 20x + 30 -> x = 3 -> ages 9 and 12.
4. THE DIRECT FORMULA (worth memorising — it turns the whole question into one line). If the present ratio is a:b and at time t the ratio is c:d, then x = t(c - d) / (ad - bc), where t is POSITIVE for 'after t years' and NEGATIVE for 't years ago'. Check: present 3:4, after 6 years 5:6 -> x = 6(5-6)/(3x6 - 4x5) = -6/-2 = 3. Correct. Present 4:5, after 5 years 5:6 -> x = 5(5-6)/(4x6 - 5x5) = -5/-1 = 5 -> ages 20 and 25. Correct.
5. THE DIFFERENCE OF TWO AGES IS CONSTANT FOREVER. This is the master lever. If A is 6 years older than B today, A - B = 6 at every point in the past and future. Use it whenever the question mixes a ratio with an absolute gap: 'ages are 5x and 8x and the difference is 12' -> 3x = 12 -> x = 4.
6. SUM-AND-CONDITION TYPE: 'the sum of present ages of father and son is 60; six years ago the father was five times the son.' F + S = 60 and F - 6 = 5(S - 6). Substitute F = 60 - S: 54 - S = 5S - 30 -> 6S = 84 -> S = 14, F = 46.
7. THREE-PERSON: identify which two are in the ratio and which one is tied by an absolute statement. Solve the ratio pair first, then plug in.
8. BACK-SUBSTITUTE FROM OPTIONS when the options are ages. Testing one option against the stated past/future condition takes 10 seconds and often beats forming the equation.
9. FINALLY, RE-READ WHAT IS ASKED: present age, age after n years, the sum, the difference, or the ratio. The options always contain more than one of these.
tricks: The direct formula x = t(c-d)/(ad-bc) with signed t answers the standard two-ratio question in one line — roughly 25 seconds saved over setting up and expanding a cross-multiplication.
Constant difference: divide the absolute age gap by the difference of the ratio parts to get one part instantly. Ratio 5:8 with a gap of 12 -> one part = 4.
When BOTH 'n years ago' and 'n years hence' appear, subtract the two equations — the constants cancel and you are left with a single term.
Option back-substitution is legitimately fast here because verifying is a subtraction and a multiplication. Try the middle option first and use the direction of the miss to jump to the right one.
If the two ratios move in the 'wrong' direction (the ratio should always drift towards 1:1 as time passes forward), you have misread which ratio is present and which is past. Free error check.
traps: Applying the time shift to only one person. Always write the shifted row for everyone before forming the equation.
The ratio given is for PAST ages while the question asks for PRESENT ages — or vice versa. Underline the tense in both the given and the asked.
'A is twice as old as B' means A = 2B. 'A is older than B by twice B's age' means A = 3B. IBPS uses both phrasings.
Answering the present age when the question asks for the age after 5 years, or asking for the sum when you computed one age. Both values are in the options.
In three-person problems, assuming the third person is part of the ratio when the question only ties them by an absolute statement.

q-pld-1.topicName: Profit, Loss & Discount I — CP, SP and percentage basics
q-pld-1.whatItIs: The arithmetic of buying and selling. Cost Price (CP) is what the seller paid, Selling Price (SP) is what the buyer paid. Profit = SP − CP, Loss = CP − SP, and in every IBPS question the percentage is calculated ON THE COST PRICE unless the question says otherwise in so many words. The single relation that generates everything is SP = CP × (100 + P%)/100, where P% is negative for a loss. This first half covers the direct forms: find any one of CP / SP / profit%, the 'if he had sold for Rs.X more' family, the two-articles-same-SP family, the 'CP of a articles = SP of b articles' family, and the dishonest-dealer false-weight family. Marked price and discount chains are the second half (q-pld-2). Questions appear as standalone word problems in Prelims and inside the Mains arithmetic mix and occasionally as a Data Sufficiency pair.
q-pld-1.coreMethod:
THE MULTIPLIER ENGINE — 4 steps, use it for every question:
1. Convert the percentage to a FRACTION from the memorised table, not a decimal. 25%=1/4, 20%=1/5, 16⅔%=1/6, 14²/₇%=1/7, 12½%=1/8, 11⅑%=1/9, 10%=1/10, 9¹/₁₁%=1/11, 8⅓%=1/12, 6¼%=1/16.
2. Turn it into a CP : SP ratio. A profit of 1/n means CP : SP = n : n+1. A loss of 1/n means CP : SP = n : n−1. So 25% profit is CP:SP = 4:5; 20% loss is CP:SP = 5:4.
3. Multiply or divide in that ratio. Going CP→SP multiply by SP/CP; going SP→CP multiply by CP/SP. There is no dividing by 100 anywhere.
4. If the question is purely percentages with no rupee figure, set CP = 100 (or CP = the LCM of the denominators involved) and read the answer straight off.

WORKED EXAMPLES (each one computed and checked):

A. Direct. An article is sold for Rs.1,120 at a profit of 12%. Find CP.
12% profit → CP:SP = 100:112 = 25:28. CP = 1120 × 25/28 = 1,000. Check: 1000 + 12% = 1,120. ✓

B. The 'Rs.X more' family. A man sells an article at a 20% loss. Had he sold it for Rs.140 more he would have gained 15%. Find CP.
Both percentages sit on the SAME base (CP), so the gap between the two selling prices is 20% + 15% = 35% of CP. 35% of CP = 140 → CP = 400. Check: 20% loss SP = 320; 320 + 140 = 460 = 400 × 1.15. ✓

C. Two articles, same SP. Two articles are sold at Rs.960 each, one at 20% profit and one at 20% loss. Overall result?
CP1 = 960 × 5/6 = 800. CP2 = 960 × 5/4 = 1,200. Total CP = 2,000, total SP = 1,920 → loss Rs.80 → 4% loss. Confirms the standard result: equal SP at ±x% is ALWAYS a loss of x²/100 % = 400/100 = 4%. ✓

D. Articles-equated family. The profit on selling 15 articles equals the selling price of 3 articles. Find profit%.
SP(15) − CP(15) = SP(3) → SP(12) = CP(15) → SP/CP = 15/12 = 5/4 → profit 25%. ✓

E. Buy-and-sell-in-lots. A man buys 12 oranges for Rs.10 and sells 10 oranges for Rs.12. Find profit%.
CP per orange = 10/12 = 5/6. SP per orange = 12/10 = 6/5. SP/CP = (6/5) ÷ (5/6) = 36/25 → profit = 11/25 = 44%. ✓

F. False weight. A dealer sells at cost price but uses a 900 g weight for 1 kg. Find gain%.
Gain% = error / (true weight − error) × 100 = 100/900 × 100 = 11⅑%. Check with the multiplier engine: he pays for 900 g, charges for 1000 g, so CP:SP = 900:1000 = 9:10, which is a 1/9 gain = 11⅑%. ✓
tricks: Fraction-first, always. 12½% of 4,800 via 1/8 is one division (600); via 0.125 it is a three-digit multiplication. Over 12 arithmetic questions this alone returns two to three minutes in a 20-minute sectional clock.

The articles-equated shortcut: if CP of a articles = SP of b articles, then profit% = (a − b)/b × 100. Check against worked example D — CP of 15 = SP of 12 gives (15−12)/12 = 25%, matching the long method. It turns a 45-second question into a 12-second one.

Equal-SP theorem: two articles sold at the SAME selling price, one at +x% and one at −x%, always produce a net LOSS of x²/100 percent. It is a proved identity, not a tendency — at ±10% the loss is 1%, at ±20% it is 4%, at ±25% it is 6.25%.

In 'sold for Rs.X more/less' problems, add the two percentages ONLY after confirming both are on CP — then the rupee gap divided by the summed percentage gives CP in one step. Worked example B is a 15-second question this way.

False-weight formula: gain% = error/(true value − error) × 100. Using 800 g for a kilo gives 200/800 = 25%; using 1,200 g when buying gives 200/1,200 = 16⅔%. Memorise the two directions (short-weighing when selling, over-taking when buying) rather than re-deriving under the clock.
When only percentages appear and no rupee figure, put CP = 100 and stop worrying about elegance — the answer will be a percentage anyway and the arithmetic becomes mental.
traps: Computing the percentage on SP instead of CP. If CP = 400 and SP = 500, the profit is 25% (100/400), not 20% (100/500). Both numbers will sit in the five options waiting for you.

Adding percentages that sit on different bases. In worked example B, 20 + 15 = 35 works because both are on CP. If one figure were 'a 15% gain on selling price', the addition is invalid and you must convert to a common base first.

Answering 'no profit no loss' on the equal-SP ±x% question. The +x% article has a smaller CP than the −x% article, so the loss on the bigger cost outweighs the gain on the smaller one. It is always a loss.

Confusing 'profit on selling 15 articles equals the SP of 3 articles' with 'profit on 15 articles equals the CP of 3 articles'. The first gives 25%, the second gives SP(15) = CP(18) → 20%. One word changes the answer.
In lot problems ('12 for Rs.10, sells 10 for Rs.12'), inverting one of the two rates. Write both as rupees-per-unit in the same direction before dividing, or the 44% becomes 20%.

Treating a false-weight gain as equal to the percentage error. Selling with a 900 g weight is an 11⅑% gain, not a 10% gain — the denominator is what he actually gave, 900, not the 1,000 he charged for.

q-pld-2.topicName: Profit, Loss & Discount II — successive discount, marked price and cost price
q-pld-2.whatItIs: The second half of the trading chain, where a third price enters. Marked Price (MP, also called list price, printed price or labelled price) is the tag on the item. Discount is always taken OFF THE MARKED PRICE. Profit is always measured AGAINST THE COST PRICE. The whole topic is one chain read left to right: CP → (mark up) → MP → (discount) → SP, and every question hands you two links and asks for the third. Successive discounts are simply two or more multipliers applied one after another to MP. The examiner's whole design here rests on the two different bases — a candidate who applies a discount to CP, or a markup to MP, produces a number that is sitting in the option list.
q-pld-2.coreMethod:
THE CHAIN METHOD — 5 steps:
1. Draw the chain on your rough sheet: CP → MP → SP. Three boxes.
2. Write the master relation: MP × (1 − d₁/100) × (1 − d₂/100) = SP = CP × (1 + p/100). Discounts multiply on the left of SP, profit multiplies on the right.
3. Convert every percentage to a fraction multiplier and cancel: 10% off = ×9/10, 12½% off = ×7/8, 15% off = ×17/20, 20% off = ×4/5, 25% off = ×3/4, 33⅓% off = ×2/3, 40% off = ×3/5. A 25% markup = ×5/4, 40% markup = ×7/5, 50% markup = ×3/2.
4. If no rupee figure is given, set CP = 100 when the question asks for profit%, and set MP = 100 when the question asks only about discounts. Never set both.
5. Read the answer off the chain. If the question asks for the EQUIVALENT SINGLE DISCOUNT, remember it is 100 minus the surviving percentage, not the surviving percentage itself.

SUCCESSIVE-DISCOUNT SHORTCUT: two discounts of a% and b% are equivalent to a single discount of (a + b − ab/100)%. For 20% and 10%: 30 − 2 = 28%. For 25% and 20%: 45 − 5 = 40%. For 10% and 10%: 20 − 1 = 19%.

THE BRIDGE FORMULA (the most useful line in the topic):
MP/CP = (100 + profit%) / (100 − discount%)
Given any two of markup, profit and discount, the third falls out in one step.

WORKED EXAMPLES (all computed and verified):

A. Straight chain. MP = Rs.2,000, successive discounts of 25% and 20%. Find SP and the equivalent single discount.
SP = 2000 × 3/4 × 4/5 = 1,200. Equivalent single discount = (2000 − 1200)/2000 = 40%. Shortcut check: 25 + 20 − (25×20)/100 = 45 − 5 = 40%. ✓

B. Markup then discount → profit. A shopkeeper marks his goods 40% above cost and allows a 25% discount. Find profit%.
CP = 100 → MP = 140 → SP = 140 × 3/4 = 105 → profit 5%. Bridge check: MP/CP = 140/100 = 1.4 and (100+5)/(100−25) = 105/75 = 1.4. ✓

C. Reverse direction. A trader wants a 20% profit after allowing a 20% discount. By what percent above cost must he mark the goods?
CP = 100 → SP must be 120 → MP = 120 ÷ 4/5 = 150 → mark up 50%. Bridge check: 120/80 = 150/100. ✓ Note that 20% up and 20% down do NOT cancel.

D. Find the missing discount. On an article marked Rs.800, two successive discounts of 20% and x% give a selling price of Rs.544. Find x.
800 × 4/5 = 640. 544/640 = 17/20 = 0.85, so the second multiplier is 85% → x = 15%. ✓

E. Discount and profit together. After allowing a 10% discount an article still yields an 8% profit. If CP is Rs.500, find MP.
SP = 500 × 27/25 = 540. MP = 540 ÷ 9/10 = 600. ✓ Bridge check: MP/CP = 600/500 = 1.2 and 108/90 = 1.2. ✓

F. Three multipliers. MP = Rs.1,600 with discounts of 25%, 20% and a further 10% cash discount on the reduced amount.
1600 × 3/4 × 4/5 × 9/10 = 864. Equivalent single discount = (1600 − 864)/1600 = 46%. Note it is NOT 25 + 20 + 10 = 55%. ✓
tricks: The bridge formula MP/CP = (100 + profit%)/(100 − discount%) answers the three commonest question types in one line each. In worked example C it replaces a three-step chain with a single division, saving roughly 25 seconds per question.

Successive discounts commute — 20% then 10% gives exactly the same selling price as 10% then 20%, because you are multiplying the same two fractions. Use that freedom to apply whichever discount cancels against your marked price first, so you never carry an ugly intermediate number.

Compute the SURVIVING fraction, not the discount, all the way through: 25% and 20% off is ×3/4 × 4/5 = 3/5 surviving. Then convert once at the end: 3/5 surviving = 40% discount. One conversion instead of two, and the cancellation is usually visible by eye.

For 'equal successive discounts of x% twice', the single equivalent is 2x − x²/100: two 10%s give 19%, two 20%s give 36%, two 25%s give 43.75%. Knowing the first two by heart covers a lot of exam questions instantly.

Set MP = 100 for pure-discount questions and CP = 100 for profit questions. Choosing the right anchor is worth about 15 seconds — anchoring at CP in a three-discount question forces you to carry fractions you never needed.
When the numbers are awkward, anchor at the LCM instead of 100: for discounts of 12½% and 20%, take MP = 400 (divisible by 8 and 5) and every intermediate stays a whole number.
traps: Adding successive discounts. 20% and 10% is 28%, not 30%. Three discounts of 25%, 20% and 10% is 46%, not 55%. The additive answer is deliberately placed in the option list every single time.

Applying the discount to cost price. Discount is defined as MP − SP and has no relationship to CP. If a question ever says 'discount on cost price', re-read it — you have almost certainly read a markup as a discount.
Assuming a 20% markup is cancelled by a 20% discount. Marking up 20% and discounting 20% gives 100 → 120 → 96, a 4% LOSS, because the two percentages act on different bases.
Reporting the surviving percentage as the answer to 'find the equivalent single discount'. In worked example A the surviving fraction is 60% and the discount is 40%; both numbers will be options.
Missing that a 'cash discount' or 'additional discount for immediate payment' is a THIRD multiplier applied to the already-reduced price, not an addition to the earlier discounts (worked example F).
Reading 'the shopkeeper marks his goods at 40% above the selling price' as 'above the cost price'. The base word after 'above' decides the entire chain — circle it before you write anything.

q-si.whatItIs: Interest computed only on the original principal, never on interest already earned. SI = P × R × T / 100, and Amount A = P + SI = P(1 + RT/100), where P is the principal in rupees, R the rate percent per annum and T the time in years. The one structural fact that makes this topic fast is that simple interest is LINEAR: the interest earned in year 1 is exactly the interest earned in year 7. Every non-trivial exam question exploits that linearity — sums that amount to different values after different periods, sums that become n times themselves, and sums split into two parts at two different rates. In IBPS Clerk it appears both as a standalone word problem and, more often in Mains, as the second half of a comparison question against compound interest.
q-si.coreMethod:
THE RT-AS-ONE-NUMBER METHOD — 4 steps:
1. Multiply rate by time FIRST and treat the product as a single total percentage. 8% for 5 years is simply 40% of the principal. 7.5% for 4 years is 30%. 12% for 2½ years is 30%. This removes one division by 100 and one multiplication from every problem.
2. Apply that total percentage to P using a fraction where possible (40% = 2/5, 30% = 3/10, 25% = 1/4).
3. Decide from the wording whether the question wants INTEREST or AMOUNT, and circle the word before computing.
4. If time is given in months or days, convert to a fraction of a year immediately (9 months = 3/4 year, 73 days = 1/5 year) and keep it as a fraction.

THE LINEARITY METHOD — for any question giving two amounts at two times:
Yearly interest = (A₂ − A₁) / (T₂ − T₁). Then P = A₁ − T₁ × (yearly interest), and R = (yearly interest / P) × 100. Three subtractions, no equations.

THE MULTIPLE-OF-PRINCIPAL METHOD — 'a sum becomes n times itself in T years':
The interest earned equals (n − 1) × P, so R × T / 100 = n − 1, giving R = (n − 1) × 100 / T and T = (n − 1) × 100 / R.

THE TWO-PART METHOD — a sum split between two rates:
Either set up one equation in x, or use alligation on the rates with the mean rate = total interest / total principal. Both are shown below.

WORKED EXAMPLES (all computed and checked):

A. Direct. P = Rs.12,000 at 7.5% per annum for 4 years.
RT = 30%. SI = 12,000 × 3/10 = Rs.3,600. Amount = Rs.15,600. ✓

B. Two amounts, two times. A sum amounts to Rs.7,440 in 3 years and Rs.8,400 in 5 years at simple interest. Find the principal and the rate.
Difference = 8,400 − 7,440 = 960 over 2 years → yearly interest = 480. P = 7,440 − 3 × 480 = 7,440 − 1,440 = Rs.6,000. R = 480/6,000 × 100 = 8% per annum. Check: 6,000 at 8% for 5 years gives 2,400 interest, amount 8,400. ✓

C. Multiple of principal. A sum becomes 3 times itself in 16 years at simple interest. Find the rate.
Interest = 2P, so R × 16/100 = 2 → R = 12.5% per annum. Check: 12.5% × 16 = 200% of P as interest, so the amount is 3P. ✓

D. Two parts at two rates. Rs.15,000 is split into two parts, one lent at 6% and the other at 10% simple interest. The total annual interest is Rs.1,240. Find each part.
Let x be the part at 6%: 0.06x + 0.10(15,000 − x) = 1,240 → 1,500 − 0.04x = 1,240 → x = 6,500. So Rs.6,500 at 6% and Rs.8,500 at 10%. Check: 390 + 850 = 1,240. ✓
Alligation check: mean rate = 1,240/15,000 = 8.267%. Ratio = (10 − 8.267) : (8.267 − 6) = 1.733 : 2.267 = 13 : 17. 15,000 × 13/30 = 6,500. ✓ Same answer.

E. Backwards. The simple interest on a sum for 3 years at 8% per annum is Rs.2,400. Find the sum.
RT = 24%, so 24% of P = 2,400 → P = Rs.10,000. ✓

F. Rate change. A sum of Rs.8,000 is lent at 5% for the first 2 years and 9% for the next 3 years. Total interest?
8,000 × 10% + 8,000 × 27% = 800 + 2,160 = Rs.2,960. Because SI never compounds, the two blocks simply add. ✓
tricks: Collapse R and T into one percentage before touching the principal. '9% for 2 years 8 months' becomes 9 × 8/3 = 24% of P — one multiplication instead of a three-term fraction. Across a full paper this is the single largest time saving in the topic.

R and T are interchangeable in simple interest: 4% for 6 years and 6% for 4 years give identical interest. When a question asks 'at what rate would the same interest be earned in 5 years instead of 8', you can swap rather than re-solve.

For 'becomes n times in T years', use R = (n − 1) × 100 / T directly. Doubling in 8 years is 12.5%; tripling in 16 years is 12.5% as well (worked example C). Two related questions collapse into one formula.

When two different multiples are given ('doubles in 8 years, in how many years does it become 5 times'), use (n₁ − 1)/T₁ = (n₂ − 1)/T₂. Here 1/8 = 4/T₂ → T₂ = 32 years. No principal and no rate needed at all.

In two-amounts-at-two-times problems, never set up simultaneous equations. Subtract the amounts, divide by the year gap, and you have the yearly interest — the principal then comes from one more subtraction (worked example B is a 25-second question this way).
For two-part lending, alligation on the RATES gives the split ratio directly; it is faster than the equation whenever the two rates are integers and the mean is easy.
traps: Treating a stated AMOUNT as the principal. 'A sum amounts to Rs.7,440 in 3 years' means principal plus interest equals 7,440. Plugging 7,440 in as P produces a number that is sitting in the option list.
Leaving time in months when the rate is per annum. 9 months is 3/4 of a year, not 9. This is the most common single arithmetic error in the topic and it inflates the answer twelve-fold.
Reading 'the sum doubles' as 'interest equals 2P'. Doubling means the AMOUNT is 2P, so the interest is only 1P. Tripling means interest = 2P. Always subtract one from the multiple.

Halving the rate and doubling the time because the question says interest is 'payable half-yearly'. That adjustment belongs to compound interest. Simple interest is unaffected by the payment frequency — the answer is identical.
In two-part problems, applying the total interest to only one part. In worked example D the Rs.1,240 is the combined annual interest on both Rs.6,500 and Rs.8,500.

Mixing SI and CI within one Mains comparison question — computing the first-year interest correctly (they are equal) and then carrying it forward as if the second year also matched. They diverge from year 2 onwards.

q-si.aiPrompt:
Act as a question setter for IBPS Clerk Prelims and Mains 2026, Numerical Ability. Generate 15 simple-interest questions.

STRICT FORMAT RULES:
- Every question must have EXACTLY FIVE options labelled (1) to (5). Exactly one is correct.
- Distribute as: 4 direct (find P, R, T or SI given the rest), 3 of the 'amounts to Rs.A1 in t1 years and Rs.A2 in t2 years' type, 3 of the 'becomes n times itself in T years' type, 3 two-part lending at two different rates with the combined interest given, 2 with the rate changing partway through the period.
- Include at least three questions where the time is stated in months (e.g. 9 months, 2 years 6 months) so the year-conversion trap is live.
- In every question, place both the INTEREST and the AMOUNT among the five options where the question asks for only one of them.

SOLUTION RULES:
- SOLVE EVERY QUESTION YOURSELF FIRST and print the full working. The correct value must be one of the five printed options — verify numerically for all 15.
- Choose numbers so that principals are round (multiples of 500 or 1,000), rates are integers or halves (6%, 7.5%, 12.5%), and all interest amounts come out as exact rupee figures. Regenerate any question producing a recurring decimal.
- In each solution, first collapse rate x time into a single percentage of the principal, then apply it. Do not use the P*R*T/100 formula mechanically when the collapse is faster.
- For the two-amount questions, solve by the difference method (subtract the two amounts, divide by the year gap) and state the yearly interest explicitly.
- State clearly in every solution whether the final answer is interest or amount.
q-si.blockPlan: One 4-hour day, ideally scheduled the day before compound interest so the contrast is fresh. Block 1 (60 min): derive SI = PRT/100 and the amount relation, drill the RT-collapse on 30 rapid conversions ('8% for 5 years = ?% of P'), then 15 direct questions untimed. Block 2 (60 min): linearity — the two-amounts-at-two-times family, 20 questions, all solved by subtraction with no algebra allowed. Then the multiple-of-principal family, 15 questions using R = (n−1)x100/T. Block 3 (60 min): two-part lending, 15 questions solved twice each — once by equation, once by alligation — so you learn which is faster for which numbers. Then 10 changing-rate questions. Block 4 (60 min): a 25-question timed set at 35 seconds each; then rewrite from memory the four method-lines (RT collapse, difference method, multiple formula, alligation) on one card for revision. Refresh with 10 questions a week inside mixed practice.

q-ci.whatItIs: Interest computed on the principal plus all interest accumulated so far, so the base grows each period. Amount A = P(1 + R/100)^n, and Compound Interest CI = A − P, where n is the number of compounding periods. At IBPS Clerk level the exponent is almost always 2 or 3, and the rates are chosen from the friendly family (5%, 8⅓%, 10%, 12½%, 20%, 25%) precisely so the arithmetic can be done by hand in under a minute. Beyond the plain calculation, three sub-forms recur: the difference between CI and SI on the same sum, half-yearly or quarterly compounding, and equal annual instalments. Compounding frequency is the exam's favourite lever: 'compounded half-yearly' halves the rate and doubles the number of periods.
q-ci.coreMethod:
THE FRACTION-MULTIPLIER METHOD — 4 steps (use this as the default):
1. Convert the rate to a growth fraction: 5% → ×21/20, 8⅓% → ×13/12, 10% → ×11/10, 12½% → ×9/8, 16⅔% → ×7/6, 20% → ×6/5, 25% → ×5/4.
2. Multiply the principal by that fraction once per period, cancelling as you go. IBPS chooses principals divisible by the denominator raised to the power n, so every intermediate is a whole number.
3. Subtract the principal at the end if the question asks for interest rather than amount.
4. Circle 'amount' or 'interest' in the question before you start — both appear in the five options.

THE TOTAL-PERCENTAGE METHOD — for 2-year questions, faster still:
Two years at R% is a total growth of (2R + R²/100)%. Memorise: 5% → 10.25%, 10% → 21%, 12½% → 26.5625%, 20% → 44%, 25% → 56.25%. One multiplication and you are done.
For three years, apply the two-year figure and then the rate once more using a + b + ab/100.

THE CI − SI DIFFERENCE FORMULAE:
For 2 years: difference = P × (R/100)².
For 3 years: difference = P × (R/100)² × (300 + R)/100.
These are different formulae — using the 2-year one on a 3-year question is the topic's commonest error.

COMPOUNDING FREQUENCY: half-yearly → rate becomes R/2 and periods become 2n. Quarterly → R/4 and 4n. Do this substitution FIRST, before any arithmetic.

WORKED EXAMPLES (all computed and checked):

A. Plain 2-year CI. P = Rs.8,000 at 10% per annum for 2 years.
8,000 × 11/10 × 11/10 = Rs.9,680, so CI = Rs.1,680. Total-percentage check: 21% of 8,000 = 1,680. ✓

B. Awkward-looking rate made easy. P = Rs.6,400 at 12½% per annum for 2 years.
6,400 × 9/8 × 9/8 = 6,400 × 81/64 = Rs.8,100. CI = Rs.1,700. ✓ (Note how the fraction turns a hostile rate into two clean divisions.)

C. CI − SI, two years. The difference between CI and SI on a sum for 2 years at 8% per annum is Rs.128. Find the sum.
P × (8/100)² = 128 → P × 64/10,000 = 128 → P = Rs.20,000. Check: SI = 20,000 × 16% = 3,200; CI = 20,000 × 1.08² − 20,000 = 23,328 − 20,000 = 3,328; difference = 128. ✓

D. Consecutive amounts → find rate and principal. A sum amounts to Rs.9,680 in 2 years and Rs.10,648 in 3 years at compound interest. Find the rate and the sum.
The third-year interest is 10,648 − 9,680 = 968, earned on 9,680, so R = 968/9,680 × 100 = 10%. Then P = 9,680 ÷ (11/10)² = 9,680 × 100/121 = Rs.8,000. ✓ (Consistent with example A.)

E. Half-yearly. Rs.12,000 at 10% per annum compounded half-yearly for 1 year.
Rate becomes 5% per half-year, periods become 2. A = 12,000 × 21/20 × 21/20 = Rs.13,230. CI = Rs.1,230. Note that annual compounding would have given only Rs.1,200. ✓

F. CI − SI, three years. P = Rs.5,000 at 10% per annum for 3 years.
CI: 5,000 × 1.331 = 6,655 → CI = 1,655. SI = 5,000 × 30% = 1,500. Difference = Rs.155. Formula check: 5,000 × (10/100)² × 310/100 = 5,000 × 0.01 × 3.1 = 155. ✓

G. Changing rate. Rs.10,000 at 10% in the first year and 12% in the second.
10,000 × 11/10 × 28/25 = 11,000 × 28/25 = Rs.12,320. CI = Rs.2,320. This is NOT the same as 11% for two years, which would give 12,321. ✓
tricks: Learn the two-year growth percentages by heart (10% → 21%, 20% → 44%, 25% → 56.25%, 5% → 10.25%). A two-year CI question then becomes a single multiplication and lands in about 20 seconds instead of 50.

The fastest CI − SI check for 2 years: the difference equals the FIRST YEAR'S interest multiplied by R%. At 10% on Rs.8,000 the first-year interest is 800, so the difference is 80 — and indeed CI 1,680 minus SI 1,600 equals 80. It matches P(R/100)² exactly and is easier to do mentally.

Two consecutive amounts hand you the rate for free: R% = (Aₙ₊₁ − Aₙ) / Aₙ × 100, because the gap between consecutive amounts is one year's interest on the earlier amount. Worked example D is a 20-second question using this.

Choose fraction multipliers over decimals whenever the rate is 8⅓%, 12½%, 16⅔% or 6¼%. Multiplying by 9/8 twice is trivial; multiplying by 1.125 twice by hand is not, and the decimal route is where careless errors enter.
For half-yearly and quarterly, write the substituted rate and period on your rough sheet BEFORE any calculation — 'R = 5, n = 2' — so you cannot half-apply the adjustment.

When the principal is not divisible by the denominator, scale: for 12½% take P in multiples of 64 for 2 years and 512 for 3 years. If the given principal is not, work with the growth percentage instead of the fraction.
traps: Applying the 2-year CI − SI formula P(R/100)² to a 3-year question. The 3-year formula carries an extra factor of (300 + R)/100 — at 10% that is 3.1 times larger, as worked examples C and F show side by side.

Half-yearly compounding: halving the rate but forgetting to double the number of periods, or doubling the periods while leaving the rate at the annual figure. Either half of the adjustment alone gives a wrong answer that appears in the options.
Averaging two different annual rates. 10% then 12% is not 11% for two years — worked example G gives Rs.12,320 against Rs.12,321. The gap is small by design, so the wrong answer looks defensible.
'Compound interest for the third year' means A₃ − A₂ only, not the total CI over three years. In worked example D the third-year interest is Rs.968 while the three-year CI is Rs.2,648.

Reporting the AMOUNT when the question asks for the INTEREST. In worked example A both 9,680 and 1,680 will be options, and under a 20-minute sectional clock this misread is more common than any arithmetic slip.

Assuming SI and CI are equal for the first year and therefore treating a one-year CI question as needing the compound formula. For n = 1 they genuinely are equal — but only for n = 1, and only when compounding is annual. If it is half-yearly, one year of CI already exceeds one year of SI (worked example E: Rs.1,230 against Rs.1,200).
