q-timework.whatItIs: How long a job takes when people of different speeds work on it, together or in sequence. One person who finishes a job in d days does 1/d of it per day — but you should almost never write that fraction. The exam-speed approach assigns the whole job a convenient number of UNITS (the LCM of the given days), which turns every rate into a whole number and every combination into simple addition. The topic covers: combined work, one person leaving or joining partway, efficiency comparisons ('twice as fast', '50% more efficient'), alternate-day working, the men-days scaling relation M₁D₁H₁/W₁ = M₂D₂H₂/W₂, and wage distribution. Pipes and cistern (q-pipes) is the same engine with negative rates, so mastering this topic makes that one nearly free.
q-timework.coreMethod:
THE LCM-UNITS METHOD — 4 steps, use it for every single question:
1. TOTAL WORK = LCM of all the day-figures given in the question. If A takes 12 days and B takes 18, total work = 36 units.
2. EFFICIENCY of each worker = total work ÷ their days. A = 36/12 = 3 units/day, B = 36/18 = 2 units/day.
3. COMBINE by adding efficiencies for everyone working simultaneously. A + B = 5 units/day. Subtract for anyone undoing work.
4. TIME = work remaining ÷ combined efficiency. 36/5 = 7.2 days.
No fractions appear anywhere. This is the whole topic.

TWO SUPPORTING RELATIONS:
• Efficiency is INVERSELY proportional to time. If A is twice as efficient as B, A's efficiency : B's = 2 : 1, so A's time : B's time = 1 : 2. '50% more efficient' means efficiency ratio 3 : 2 and time ratio 2 : 3.
• Man-days scaling: M₁ × D₁ × H₁ / W₁ = M₂ × D₂ × H₂ / W₂. Use it whenever the number of workers changes and no individual rate is given.

WAGES: split in the ratio of WORK ACTUALLY DONE, which is efficiency × number of days each person worked. Never in the ratio of days taken.

WORKED EXAMPLES (all computed and checked):

A. Basic combination. A does a job in 12 days, B in 18 days. Together?
LCM = 36. A = 3, B = 2, together = 5/day. Time = 36/5 = 7.2 days = 7⅕ days. ✓

B. Backing out one worker. A and B together finish in 8 days; A alone takes 12 days. B alone?
LCM = 24. Together = 3/day, A = 2/day, so B = 1/day → B alone takes 24 days. ✓

C. Efficiency ratio. A is twice as efficient as B and together they finish in 14 days. A alone?
A : B = 2 : 1, so combined = 3 units/day. Total work = 3 × 14 = 42 units. A alone = 42/2 = 21 days. Check: B alone = 42 days; 1/21 + 1/42 = 3/42 = 1/14. ✓

D. Someone leaves. A, B and C can do a job in 10, 12 and 15 days. All three start together but A leaves after 2 days. How long does the whole job take?
LCM = 60. A = 6, B = 5, C = 4. First 2 days at 15/day = 30 units done. Remaining 30 units at 9/day (B + C) = 30/9 = 3⅓ days. Total = 5⅓ days. ✓

E. Man-days scaling. 12 men complete a job in 18 days. After 6 days, 4 more men join. How many MORE days to finish?
Total = 12 × 18 = 216 man-days. Done in 6 days = 72 man-days. Remaining = 144 man-days with 16 men = 9 days. ✓

F. Alternate days. A can do a job in 9 days and B in 18 days. They work on alternate days starting with A. Total time?
LCM = 18. A = 2/day, B = 1/day. Each 2-day block = 3 units. Five blocks (10 days) = 15 units. Day 11 is A's: 15 + 2 = 17. Day 12 is B's: 17 + 1 = 18 units — complete. Total = 12 days. ✓

G. Wages. A alone can do a job in 6 days, B alone in 8 days. With C's help all three finish in 3 days. The total wage is Rs.3,200. What is C's share?
LCM = 24. A = 4, B = 3, all three = 24/3 = 8/day. So C = 8 − 4 − 3 = 1/day. Wage ratio A : B : C = 4 : 3 : 1. C's share = 3,200 × 1/8 = Rs.400. ✓
tricks: Never write 1/12 + 1/18. Setting total work to the LCM removes every fraction from the page and turns a 60-second question into a 30-second one; the arithmetic error rate collapses along with the time.

For alternate-day problems, compute the 2-day block first, divide the total by the block, then finish the tail one day at a time. Crucially, check whether the job completes MID-DAY: if 2 units remain and the worker on duty does 3 per day, the answer carries a half-day (e.g. 11.5 days), and that fraction will be one of the five options.

Efficiency ratio inverts to time ratio, so 'A is thrice as efficient as B' means B takes three times as long. Set the combined efficiency as the sum of the ratio parts and multiply by the given joint time to get total work in one step — worked example C never needs individual days.

Man-days is a conserved quantity when no individual rates are given: total man-days done plus total man-days remaining equals the original product. Worked example E takes two subtractions and one division, with no LCM needed at all.

Wages follow work done, so once you have the efficiency figures the wage ratio is already on your page — no extra computation. In worked example G, finding C's efficiency (1 unit) and the total (8 units) is the entire question.

When a question says 'A leaves 3 days BEFORE the work is completed', let T be the total time: A works for T − 3 days and the others for T. Set up units-done = total and solve for T. This differs structurally from 'A leaves after 3 days' and needs the variable.
traps: Splitting wages in the ratio of DAYS TAKEN instead of work done. If A takes 6 days and B takes 8, the wage ratio is 4 : 3 (their efficiencies), not 6 : 8. The inverted answer is always among the options.
Confusing 'A is twice as efficient as B' with 'A takes twice as long as B'. These are opposite statements and produce reciprocal answers.
Adding times instead of efficiencies. A at 12 days and B at 18 days together take 7.2 days, not 30 and not 15. Only rates add.

In alternate-day problems, ignoring who starts. Nine days for A and eighteen for B starting with A gives 12 days (worked example F); starting with B the first 10 days give 15 units, day 11 (A) gives 17, day 12 (B) gives 18 — also 12 days here, but with unequal efficiencies and a different total the two orders often differ by a day, so always re-check the tail rather than assuming symmetry.

'A leaves after 3 days' versus 'A leaves 3 days before completion' — the first is a fixed 3 days of A's work, the second is an unknown that must be solved for. Reading one as the other changes the answer entirely.
In man-days questions, adding the extra workers from day one instead of from the day they joined. In worked example E the 16 men work only the final stretch; the first 6 days are at 12 men.

q-pipes.whatItIs: Time and work wearing a different costume. A pipe that fills a tank in t hours works at 1/t of the tank per hour; a pipe that empties it works at −1/t. Every question is a matter of adding positive and negative rates and dividing the capacity by the net rate. The recurring sub-forms are: several pipes open together, a leak that slows a filling pipe, a pipe closed partway through, pipes opened alternately for one minute each, capacity questions where an inlet is quoted in litres per minute, and tanks that start partly filled. Because the machinery is identical to q-timework, this topic is cheap to add once that one is done — the only genuinely new content is sign discipline.
q-pipes.coreMethod:
THE SIGNED-LCM METHOD — 5 steps:
1. CAPACITY = LCM of all the given fill and empty times. Write it in a box at the top.
2. RATE of each pipe = capacity ÷ its time. Write inlet rates as POSITIVE and outlet or leak rates as NEGATIVE, in a single column so the signs are visible.
3. NET RATE = the algebraic sum of the pipes that are actually open during the period you are considering.
4. CHECK THE SIGN of the net rate before dividing. Positive means the tank fills; negative means it empties and a question asking 'time to fill' has no positive answer — the option list will contain 'cannot be filled' or 'never'.
5. TIME = (work remaining) ÷ (net rate). 'Work remaining' is the full capacity only if the tank starts empty — read for words like 'half full' or 'one-third filled'.

THE LEAK SHORTCUT: if a pipe alone fills in t₁ hours but takes t₂ hours because of a leak, the leak alone empties a full tank in t₁t₂/(t₂ − t₁) hours.

UNITS DISCIPLINE: when one rate is in litres per minute and another is per hour, convert to a single time unit BEFORE writing the equation. This is where litre-capacity questions are won or lost.

WORKED EXAMPLES (all computed and checked):

A. Three pipes, one outlet. Pipe A fills a tank in 12 hours, B fills it in 15 hours and C empties it in 20 hours. All three are opened together. How long to fill?
LCM = 60. A = +5, B = +4, C = −3. Net = +6 per hour. Time = 60/6 = 10 hours. ✓

B. The leak family. A pipe can fill a tank in 6 hours, but because of a leak it takes 8 hours. How long would the leak alone take to empty a full tank?
LCM = 24. Pipe = +4, pipe-with-leak = +3, so leak = −1 per hour → 24 hours. Shortcut check: 6 × 8 / (8 − 6) = 48/2 = 24 hours. ✓

C. A pipe closed partway. Two pipes fill a tank in 20 minutes and 30 minutes respectively. Both are opened together, but the first is closed after some time and the tank is full in 18 minutes altogether. After how many minutes was the first pipe closed?
LCM = 60. A = +3, B = +2. B runs the whole 18 minutes: 2 × 18 = 36 units. The remaining 60 − 36 = 24 units came from A at 3/minute → A ran for 8 minutes. Answer: closed after 8 minutes. ✓

D. Litres per minute. A tank has a leak that would empty it in 12 hours. An inlet admitting 6 litres per minute is opened, and now the tank empties in 20 hours. Find the capacity.
Inlet = 6 litres/min = 360 litres/hour. Leak rate = C/12 per hour. Net emptying rate = C/20 per hour.
C/12 − 360 = C/20 → C(1/12 − 1/20) = 360 → C(5 − 3)/60 = 360 → C/30 = 360 → C = 10,800 litres. ✓ Check: leak drains 900 l/h, inlet adds 360 l/h, net 540 l/h, and 10,800/540 = 20 hours. ✓

E. Alternate minutes. Pipe A fills a tank in 10 minutes and pipe B in 15 minutes. They are opened alternately for one minute each, starting with A. How long to fill?
LCM = 30. A = +3, B = +2. Each 2-minute block adds 5 units. Five blocks (10 minutes) = 25 units. Minute 11 is A's: 25 + 3 = 28. Minute 12 is B's: B adds 2, reaching exactly 30. Total = 12 minutes. ✓

F. Partly-filled tank. A tank is one-third full. Pipe A fills it in 18 minutes and pipe B empties it in 9 minutes. If both are opened, will the tank fill or empty, and in how long?
LCM = 18. A = +1, B = −2. Net = −1 per minute. The tank currently holds 6 units, so it EMPTIES in 6 minutes. A question asking 'time to fill' here would be answered 'the tank can never be filled'. ✓
tricks: Write every rate in one vertical column with its sign attached, inlets above outlets. Sign errors are the only real difficulty in this topic, and a two-column layout eliminates them at the cost of about three seconds.

Use the leak shortcut t₁t₂/(t₂ − t₁) for the whole 'pipe alone versus pipe with leak' family — a 6-and-8-hour question becomes 48/2 = 24 in about ten seconds, against roughly forty seconds for the full LCM route.

For 'one pipe closed partway, tank full in T minutes', compute the always-open pipe's total contribution over the full T first, subtract from capacity, and divide the balance by the closed pipe's rate. That gives the running time directly, as in worked example C, with no equation.
Check the sign of the net rate before doing any division. If it is negative or zero, you already know the answer is 'cannot be filled' and you have saved the whole calculation.

In litres-per-minute questions, convert the inlet to litres per HOUR immediately if the leak is quoted in hours (6 l/min → 360 l/h). Doing this before writing the equation prevents the single commonest error in the capacity family.

For alternate-minute problems, compute the 2-minute block, then handle the tail minute by minute — and allow for a partial minute. If 2 units remain and the pipe on duty delivers 3 per minute, the answer is a further 2/3 of a minute, and such fractional answers do appear in the option list.
traps: Adding an outlet pipe's rate instead of subtracting it. In worked example A, treating C as an inlet gives 60/12 = 5 hours instead of 10 — and 5 hours will be one of the five options.

Assuming a tank always fills. When the outlets outrun the inlets the net rate is negative and the correct answer is that the tank cannot be filled, or that it empties. Worked example F is exactly this case.

Applying the full LCM capacity to a tank that is already partly filled. 'The tank is one-third full' means only two-thirds remains to be filled — or, if it is emptying, only one-third remains to be drained.
Mixing minutes and hours in the same rate column. A leak quoted in hours and an inlet quoted in litres per minute must be brought to a common unit before they can be combined (worked example D).

Reading 'pipe A can empty a FULL tank in 20 minutes' and applying that 20 minutes to a tank that is only half full. The stated time always refers to the full capacity; scale it to whatever is actually in the tank.
In the closed-partway family, answering with the total time (18 minutes) rather than the time the pipe ran (8 minutes), or vice versa. Circle which one the question asks for before computing.

q-pipes.aiPrompt:
Act as a question setter for IBPS Clerk Prelims and Mains 2026, Numerical Ability. Generate 15 pipes-and-cistern questions.

STRICT FORMAT RULES:
- Every question must have EXACTLY FIVE options labelled (1) to (5). Exactly one is correct.
- Distribute as: 3 with two inlets and one outlet opened together, 3 of the pipe-with-leak type, 3 where one pipe is closed partway and the total time is given, 2 capacity questions with the inlet in litres per minute and the leak in hours, 2 alternate-minute opening with the starting pipe named, 2 with the tank already part-filled (make ONE of these a case where the outlets outrun the inlets, so the correct answer is 'the tank cannot be filled').
- Choose fill/empty times whose LCM is small and friendly (12/15/20, 10/15, 6/8).
- In every question involving an outlet, place among the wrong options the value obtained by adding the outlet's rate instead of subtracting it.

SOLUTION RULES:
- SOLVE EVERY QUESTION YOURSELF FIRST and print the full working. The correct value must be one of the five printed options — verify numerically for all 15.
- Solve in LCM units, presenting each pipe's rate in a signed column (inlets positive, outlets negative) and stating the net rate before dividing. Do not write 1/a + 1/b anywhere.
- For every leak question, also verify with the shortcut t1*t2/(t2-t1) and confirm both routes agree.
- For litre-capacity questions, state the unit conversion (litres per minute to litres per hour) on its own line before the equation.
- For alternate-minute questions, show the 2-minute block, the number of complete blocks, and the tail minute by minute, stating whether the tank fills part-way through a minute.
- Answers must be whole numbers or fractions with a denominator under 12. Regenerate any question with an ugly result.
q-pipes.blockPlan: One 4-hour day, and schedule it IMMEDIATELY after q-timework so the LCM-units engine is still warm — the only new idea here is the negative sign. Block 1 (60 min): set up the signed rate column and do 20 questions with multiple inlets and one outlet, including three where the net rate is negative so you meet the 'cannot be filled' answer early rather than in the exam. Block 2 (60 min): the leak family — 15 questions by the full LCM route first, then re-do the same 15 with the t1t2/(t2−t1) shortcut and time yourself on both to feel the difference. Block 3 (60 min): closed-partway and part-filled tanks, 20 questions, always writing down how much capacity actually remains. Block 4 (60 min): litre-capacity questions with unit conversion (10 questions) and alternate-minute opening (10 questions), then a short 10-question timed mix at 50 seconds each. Thereafter fold 5-6 questions a week into mixed practice; because the engine is shared with time and work, revising one revises the other.

q-tsd.whatItIs: Every question in this family is one equation: Speed = Distance / Time. What makes it an exam topic is not the formula but the three shapes IBPS wraps around it: (a) same distance covered at two different speeds, giving a late/early time gap; (b) average speed over a journey split into parts; (c) two bodies moving toward or away from each other, where you work with relative speed. It is also the parent topic of Boats & Streams and Trains — the same three shapes reappear there with a stream or a train length added. In Clerk Prelims it shows up as a plain 2-3 line word problem; in Mains it is often bundled into an arithmetic set or a caselet with one TSD sub-question.
q-tsd.coreMethod:
1. WRITE THE UNIT FIRST. If the answer is asked in metres/seconds, convert every km/h to m/s at the very start using x5/18. If everything is in km and hours, do not convert at all. Memorise: 18 km/h = 5 m/s, 36 = 10, 54 = 15, 72 = 20, 90 = 25, 108 = 30.
2. IDENTIFY WHICH QUANTITY IS CONSTANT. In almost every question one of D, S, T is fixed. Same distance is the most common. Say it out loud: 'distance is the same'.
3. IF DISTANCE IS CONSTANT, USE INVERSE RATIO, NOT ALGEBRA. Speeds in ratio a:b means times in ratio b:a. Do not set up D/a - D/b = t; set up the ratio and match one part to the given time gap.
   Worked: walking at 5 km/h a student is 6 minutes LATE; at 6 km/h he is 4 minutes EARLY. Speeds 5:6, so times 6:5. Difference = 1 part. Actual time gap = 6 + 4 = 10 minutes, so 1 part = 10 min. Time at 5 km/h = 6 parts = 60 min = 1 hour. Distance = 5 x 1 = 5 km. (Check: 5/6 h = 50 min, which is 4 min less than the 54-min schedule. Correct.)
4. IF THE QUESTION GIVES A PERCENTAGE CHANGE IN SPEED, FLIP THE FRACTION. Speed becomes 5/4 of original (a 25% rise) means time becomes 4/5 of original (a 20% fall). Speed becomes 3/4 (25% drop) means time becomes 4/3 (a 33 1/3% rise). Never compute the distance for these.
5. AVERAGE SPEED = TOTAL DISTANCE / TOTAL TIME. Always. For two EQUAL distances at speeds a and b, the shortcut is 2ab/(a+b). For three equal parts at a, b, c it is 3abc/(ab+bc+ca).
   Worked: 60 km/h out, 40 km/h back. Average = 2(60)(40)/100 = 48 km/h.
6. IF THE TIMES ARE EQUAL INSTEAD OF THE DISTANCES, the average IS the plain average (a+b)/2. Check which one the question gave before choosing.
7. FOR TWO BODIES: moving toward each other or crossing, add the speeds; moving in the same direction (chasing), subtract. Time to meet = gap / relative speed.
8. FOR THE 'AFTER MEETING' PATTERN: two people start from opposite ends at the same time; after meeting, A needs t1 more hours and B needs t2 more hours. Then Speed A : Speed B = root(t2) : root(t1).
   Worked: after meeting A takes 4 h, B takes 9 h. Ratio = root9 : root4 = 3:2. (Verify: meeting happened at 4 x 3/2 = 6 hours.)
9. STOPPAGE QUESTIONS: if a bus runs at x km/h without stops and y km/h with stops, stoppage time per hour = (x - y)/x hours. Example: 60 and 45 gives 15/60 h = 15 minutes per hour.
tricks: Inverse-ratio in one line: for the late/early pattern, speeds a:b give times b:a, and the difference of the two time-parts equals the TOTAL of the late and early minutes. One subtraction, one division, done in about 20 seconds. Setting up D/a - D/b wastes 30-40 seconds and invites an LCM slip.

Convert once, at the start, never mid-solution. Deciding 'this is a metres-and-seconds question' before writing anything eliminates the single most common wrong answer, which is the right number in the wrong unit.

Percentage-change questions need no distance at all: speed x k means time x 1/k. 20% faster = 5/6 the time (a 16 2/3% saving); 20% slower = 5/4 the time (a 25% increase). Reading the answer straight off the reciprocal saves the whole equation.

When the five options are far apart, estimate: 2ab/(a+b) always lies strictly between a and b and always closer to the SMALLER speed. If only one option sits between the two speeds and below their plain average, that is the answer and you have spent 10 seconds.
Keep distances in the numerator as fractions, not decimals. 40/3 km/h beaten into 13.33 costs time and rounding error; carry the fraction to the last step, where it usually cancels.
traps: Adding the late and early gaps wrongly. 'Six minutes late' and 'four minutes early' is a gap of TEN minutes, not two. Aspirants who subtract get 1 km instead of 5 km in the worked example above, and 1 km is almost always one of the five options.
Treating (a+b)/2 as average speed when the two DISTANCES are equal. For 60 and 40 the answer is 48, not 50, and 50 will be one of the options specifically to catch this.

Multiplying by 18/5 when you needed 5/18. km/h to m/s is x5/18 (the number gets SMALLER); m/s to km/h is x18/5 (the number gets BIGGER). If your converted speed went up when going from km/h to m/s, you flipped it.

Leaving minutes in an equation whose other terms are in hours. '12 minutes' inside a km/h equation must be 1/5, not 12. This produces answers off by a factor of 60, which look absurd but still get circled under clock pressure.

Assuming a body that 'starts 2 hours later' covers the same time. In catch-up questions the head start is a DISTANCE (early speed x head-start hours), and that distance is what the relative speed has to eat up. Forgetting to convert the head start from hours into km is the standard error.
Applying root(t2):root(t1) when the two people did NOT start at the same moment. That result is derived assuming simultaneous start; if starts are staggered, go back to the basic equation.
q-tsd.timeTarget: Direct one-step question (find D, S or T given two of them): 25-35 seconds. Late/early or percentage-change question by the ratio method: 40-50 seconds. Average speed: 30-40 seconds. Two-body relative speed or 'after meeting': 60-75 seconds. In Prelims, if a TSD question crosses 75 seconds, leave it and move on — the 20-minute sectional clock does not forgive one stubborn question.
q-tsd.masteryCheck: You have mastered this when, given 'a man walking at 4 km/h reaches his office 8 minutes late, and at 5 km/h reaches 7 minutes early', you can write 4:5 -> times 5:4 -> 1 part = 15 min -> time at 4 km/h = 75 min = 5/4 h -> distance = 5 km, in under 40 seconds without algebra. Second check: state instantly that a 20% increase in speed cuts time by 16 2/3%, and that the average speed for equal distances at 30 and 20 km/h is 24 km/h, not 25. Third check: given 10 mixed TSD questions, you get 9 right in 10 minutes.
questionPatterns: Late/early: 'Walking at 3/4 of his usual speed, a man reaches office 20 minutes late. Find his usual time.' (Speed 3/4 -> time 4/3 -> extra 1/3 of usual time = 20 min -> usual time = 60 min.)
Average speed with equal halves: 'A car covers the first half of a 300 km journey at 50 km/h and the second half at 75 km/h. Find the average speed.' (2 x 50 x 75/125 = 60 km/h.)

Two-part journey with total time: 'A man covers 480 km partly at 40 km/h and partly at 60 km/h, taking 10 hours in all. Find the distance covered at 40 km/h.' (40t + 60(10-t) = 480 -> t = 6 h -> 240 km.)

Head start / catch-up: 'A starts at 8 a.m. at 30 km/h; B follows the same route at 10 a.m. at 45 km/h. At what time does B overtake A?' (Head start = 60 km; relative speed 15 km/h; 4 hours after 10 a.m. = 2 p.m.)
Stoppage: 'Excluding stoppages a bus averages 54 km/h; including stoppages, 45 km/h. How many minutes per hour does it stop?' ((54-45)/54 h = 10 minutes.)

After-meeting ratio: 'Two trains start simultaneously from A and B towards each other; after meeting they reach B and A in 9 and 16 hours respectively. Find the ratio of their speeds.' (root16 : root9 = 4:3.)

q-boats.whatItIs: Time, Speed & Distance with one extra term. A boat has a speed in still water (call it u) and the river has a current speed (v). Going with the current — downstream — the boat's effective speed is u+v. Going against it — upstream — it is u-v. Every question is built by hiding one or two of u, v, downstream speed or upstream speed and giving you distances and times instead. The topic is small, closed and highly formulaic, which makes it one of the fastest scoring topics in the arithmetic block once the four relations are automatic. IBPS asks it as a standalone word problem, occasionally as one arm of a two-statement quantity-comparison question in Mains.
q-boats.coreMethod:
1. DEFINE FOUR SYMBOLS ON PAPER BEFORE READING THE NUMBERS: u = still-water speed, v = stream speed, D = u+v (downstream), U = u-v (upstream).
2. THE TWO REVERSE FORMULAS ARE THE WHOLE TOPIC: u = (D+U)/2 and v = (D-U)/2. Still-water speed is the AVERAGE of the two effective speeds; stream speed is HALF THE DIFFERENCE.
   Worked: a boat covers 24 km downstream in 2 hours and returns in 3 hours. D = 24/2 = 12, U = 24/3 = 8. So u = (12+8)/2 = 10 km/h and v = (12-8)/2 = 2 km/h.
3. IF THE SAME DISTANCE TAKES t_down AND t_up: u/v = (t_up + t_down)/(t_up - t_down). Use this when the question gives times but not the distance. Check with the numbers above: (3+2)/(3-2) = 5, and indeed 10/2 = 5.
4. IF THE QUESTION SAYS 'x km downstream in the same time as y km upstream', then D:U = x:y immediately, with no equation. From D:U you get u:v = (x+y):(x-y).
   Worked: he rows 4 km with the stream in the time he rows 3 km against it, and covers 48 km each way in 14 hours total. D:U = 4:3, so let D = 4k, U = 3k. 48/4k + 48/3k = 14 -> 12/k + 16/k = 14 -> 28/k = 14 -> k = 2. So D = 8, U = 6, u = 7 km/h, v = 1 km/h.
5. FOR THE 'TAKES t HOURS MORE UPSTREAM' PATTERN, use d/(u-v) - d/(u+v) = t, which simplifies to 2dv/(u^2 - v^2) = t. Plug in and solve the quadratic in whichever variable is unknown.
   Worked: a boat takes 2 hours more to go 48 km upstream than to return downstream; stream = 2 km/h. 2(48)(2)/(u^2 - 4) = 2 -> 192 = 2u^2 - 8 -> u^2 = 100 -> u = 10 km/h. (Check: up = 8 -> 6 h; down = 12 -> 4 h; difference 2 h.)
6. ROUND-TRIP AVERAGE SPEED IS NOT u. Over a there-and-back trip of distance d each way, average speed = (u^2 - v^2)/u. With u = 10, v = 2 this is 96/10 = 9.6 km/h, not 10.
7. STILL WATER MEANS v = 0. A lake or pond question is pure TSD; do not invent a current.
8. IF THE OBJECT IS A SWIMMER, A SHIP, OR A MAN ROWING, nothing changes — the words differ, the algebra does not.
tricks: Read the sentence and immediately label each given speed as u, D or U. 'A boat travels at 12 km/h downstream' is D = 12, not u = 12. Doing this labelling before touching the arithmetic removes the single largest source of wrong answers in this topic and costs three seconds.

When both times for the same distance are given, go straight to u/v = (t_up + t_down)/(t_up - t_down) and skip computing D and U at all. On a question asking only for the RATIO, this is a single fraction and lands in about 15 seconds.

Halve-the-difference is faster than solving simultaneous equations. Given D and U, v = (D-U)/2 in one subtraction. Aspirants who write u + v = 12 and u - v = 8 and then eliminate are doing three lines of work for a one-line answer.

Use the 'same time' phrasing as a free ratio. 'Rows 4 km downstream in the time he rows 3 km upstream' hands you D:U = 4:3 with zero computation, because equal time means distance is directly proportional to speed.

For the 't hours more' pattern, note that 2dv/(u^2 - v^2) = t always produces u^2 as a clean number in IBPS papers. If your u^2 is not a perfect square, you have almost certainly mislabelled which speed is the stream — recheck rather than reaching for a calculator-style estimate.
traps: Treating the given 'speed of the boat' as still-water speed when the sentence actually described a downstream or upstream run. If the question says 'a boat covers 36 km in 3 hours going downstream', that 12 km/h is D; the still-water speed is smaller.
Computing v as (D-U) instead of (D-U)/2. In the 24 km example this gives 4 km/h instead of 2 km/h, and 4 will be among the five options.

Reporting the round-trip average speed as u. For a boat with u = 10 and v = 2 the round-trip average is 9.6 km/h; the current does not cancel out, because the slow leg takes longer and therefore carries more weight.
Mixing up which leg is longer in time. Upstream is the SLOWER leg, so it always takes MORE time. If your working has the upstream leg finishing faster, a sign is flipped.

Adding the stream speed twice — for example writing downstream speed as u + v and then, later in the same solution, adding v again to get the 'effective' speed. This shows up when a question involves a boat plus a floating object.
Forgetting that a floating object (a log, a bottle, a raft) has speed exactly v, not u+v. It has no engine; it moves at the stream's speed only.

questionPatterns: Two legs given: 'A man rows 16 km downstream in 2 hours and 9 km upstream in 3 hours. Find the speed of the stream.' (D = 8, U = 3, v = 2.5 km/h.)

Still-water speed and stream given, find time: 'A boat whose speed in still water is 9 km/h covers 45 km downstream and returns, in a stream flowing at 3 km/h. Find the total time.' (45/12 + 45/6 = 3.75 + 7.5 = 11.25 hours.)

'Same time' phrasing: 'A boat travels 20 km downstream in the same time it takes to travel 12 km upstream. If the stream flows at 4 km/h, find the boat's speed in still water.' (D:U = 20:12 = 5:3, so u:v = 8:2 = 4:1, hence u = 16 km/h.)

't hours more' pattern: 'A boat takes 3 hours more to cover 90 km upstream than downstream. If the boat's still-water speed is 12 km/h, find the stream speed.' (2 x 90 x v/(144 - v^2) = 3 -> 180v = 432 - 3v^2 -> v^2 + 60v - 144 = 0 -> v = 2.29... — reject this shape and instead solve numerically: this illustrates that not every set of numbers is clean, so always sanity-check that your quadratic factorises before committing to it.)

Times-ratio question: 'A boat takes twice as long to go upstream as to come downstream over the same distance. Find the ratio of the boat's speed in still water to the stream's speed.' (u/v = (2+1)/(2-1) = 3:1.)
Floating object: 'A boat goes 24 km downstream in 3 hours and the same distance upstream in 4 hours. How long will a log take to float 12 km downstream?' (D = 8, U = 6, v = 1 km/h, so 12 hours.)

q-trains.whatItIs: Time, Speed & Distance in which the moving body has a LENGTH. The single idea that generates every question is: the distance a train covers while 'crossing' something equals its own length plus the length of the thing it crosses. A pole, a man, a signal or a tree has zero length; a platform, a bridge, a tunnel or another train has length. Add relative speed for two trains and you have the whole topic. IBPS asks it as a standalone Prelims word problem and, in Mains, sometimes as part of a quantity-comparison or a two-variable set.
q-trains.coreMethod:
1. CONVERT TO m/s IMMEDIATELY. Lengths in these questions are in metres, so km/h must become m/s via x5/18. Memorise the six values you will actually meet: 18 -> 5, 36 -> 10, 45 -> 12.5, 54 -> 15, 72 -> 20, 90 -> 25, 108 -> 30.
2. WRITE THE CROSSING DISTANCE BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE.
   - Crossing a pole, tree, signal, or a STANDING man: distance = train length only.
   - Crossing a platform, bridge, tunnel, or another train: distance = sum of the two lengths.
3. TIME = CROSSING DISTANCE / RELEVANT SPEED. That is the only equation.
   Worked: a 180 m train at 54 km/h crosses a platform in 22 seconds. 54 km/h = 15 m/s. Distance covered = 15 x 22 = 330 m. Platform = 330 - 180 = 150 m.
4. TWO TRAINS: opposite directions -> relative speed = s1 + s2. Same direction -> relative speed = s1 - s2 (take the positive difference). Crossing distance = L1 + L2 in BOTH cases.
   Worked: trains 120 m and 180 m at 42 km/h and 30 km/h. Opposite: relative 72 km/h = 20 m/s, so 300/20 = 15 seconds. Same direction: relative 12 km/h = 10/3 m/s, so 300 x 3/10 = 90 seconds.
5. TRAIN AND A MOVING MAN: the man still has zero length, but he has speed. Use relative speed and train length only.
   Worked: a 150 m train at 63 km/h crosses a man running at 3 km/h in the SAME direction. Relative = 60 km/h = 50/3 m/s. Time = 150 x 3/50 = 9 seconds. If the man ran in the OPPOSITE direction: relative = 66 km/h.
6. POLE-THEN-PLATFORM PAIR: if a train crosses a pole in t1 seconds and a platform of length P in t2 seconds, then train length L = P x t1/(t2 - t1). Derivation: speed = L/t1 and (L+P)/t2 = L/t1.
   Worked: pole in 12 s, 250 m platform in 27 s. L = 250 x 12/15 = 200 m. Speed = 200/12 m/s = 60 km/h.
7. TWO TRAINS STARTING SIMULTANEOUSLY toward each other and reaching the far stations a and b hours after crossing: speed ratio = root(b) : root(a). This is the same result as in Time, Speed & Distance; lengths are ignored in this pattern.
8. SANITY CHECK EVERY ANSWER. A train crossing a platform must take LONGER than crossing a pole. Two trains in the same direction must take LONGER to cross than in opposite directions. If either check fails, you have a sign or a length error.
tricks: Do the x5/18 conversion on the numbers before you read the rest of the question, and write the m/s values in the margin. Every subsequent step is then a whole-number division. Converting halfway through is where the 60-second questions become 100-second questions.

For two trains, convert the RELATIVE speed rather than each speed separately. 42 + 30 = 72 km/h, then one multiplication by 5/18 gives 20 m/s. That is one conversion instead of two and removes a rounding step.
Use L = P x t1/(t2 - t1) for the pole-and-platform pair instead of setting up two equations. It turns a two-equation problem into one multiplication and lands in about 25 seconds.
When the question says 'two trains of equal length', immediately write 2L for the crossing distance and solve for L in one step, rather than carrying L1 and L2 through the algebra.

Keep m/s in thirds rather than decimals: 12 km/h is 10/3 m/s, not 3.33. The 3 nearly always cancels against a length that is a multiple of 3, and you avoid a rounding error that would push you onto a wrong option.
traps: Treating 'a man standing on a platform' as if the platform length mattered. It does not — a standing man is a point, so the crossing distance is the train's length alone. This is the most frequently exploited misreading in the topic, and the option corresponding to length-plus-platform is always present.

Using L1 + L2 for two trains but forgetting it applies to the SAME-direction case too. Whether they are approaching or overtaking, the front of one must travel past the rear of the other, so the distance is always the sum of the lengths; only the SPEED changes.

Subtracting speeds for trains moving in opposite directions. Opposite means the gap closes faster, so speeds ADD. If your 'crossing' time for opposite directions came out longer than for the same direction, you have swapped them.
Forgetting the conversion entirely and dividing 300 metres by 72 km/h. The number produced is dimensionless nonsense but will often coincide with one of the five options.
Reading 'crosses a bridge of 300 m in 30 seconds' as though 300 m were the total distance covered. The total distance is 300 plus the train's length.

Assuming a train crossing another train that is STATIONARY uses relative speed. A stationary train has speed zero, so the relative speed is just the moving train's speed — but the crossing distance is still the sum of both lengths.

questionPatterns: Pole and platform pair: 'A train crosses a pole in 15 seconds and a 240 m platform in 27 seconds. Find the length of the train.' (L = 240 x 15/12 = 300 m; speed = 20 m/s = 72 km/h.)

Standing man vs platform (the trap pattern): 'A train crosses a man standing on a 200 m platform in 9 seconds and crosses the platform itself in 24 seconds. Find the train's length.' (Man gives L/s = 9; platform gives (L+200)/s = 24; so 200/s = 15, s = 40/3 m/s, L = 120 m.)
Meeting-time pattern: 'Two trains start at the same time from stations 300 km apart and travel towards each other at 65 km/h and 35 km/h. After how long do they meet?' (300/100 = 3 hours.)

q-mixture.whatItIs: A method for combining two things with different 'per-unit values' and for tracking what happens when part of a mixture is removed and replaced. It has two distinct halves that are often confused. The first half is ALLIGATION: given two ingredients at values c (cheaper) and d (dearer) blended to a mean value m, the rule (quantity of cheaper)/(quantity of dearer) = (d - m)/(m - c) gives the mixing ratio in one line. The second half is REPLACEMENT: repeatedly removing a fixed volume of a mixture and topping up with one pure component, which follows a clean power formula. Alligation is far more than a mixtures tool — the same rule solves weighted averages of prices, interest rates, marks, ages and speeds, which is why it earns study time out of proportion to the number of questions labelled 'mixture'.
q-mixture.coreMethod:
1. ALLIGATION SETUP. Write cheaper value c on the left, dearer value d on the right, mean m in the middle. Then cheaper:dearer = (d - m) : (m - c). The differences cross over: the quantity of the CHEAPER item is proportional to the distance from the mean to the DEARER value.
   Worked: rice at Rs 30/kg mixed with rice at Rs 45/kg to sell at Rs 36/kg. Ratio = (45-36):(36-30) = 9:6 = 3:2. So 3 parts of the Rs 30 rice to 2 parts of the Rs 45 rice.
2. ALLIGATION GIVES ONLY A RATIO. To get actual quantities you need one absolute number from the question (a total weight, a total cost, one ingredient's amount). If none is given, the answer being asked for must itself be a ratio.
3. WHEN THE 'VALUE' IS A FRACTION, USE THE FRACTION. For milk-water problems, take the fraction of MILK in each vessel as the value.
   Worked: vessel A has milk:water = 5:3 (milk fraction 5/8), vessel B has 3:5 (milk fraction 3/8). Mix to get 1:1 (milk fraction 4/8). Ratio = (5/8 - 4/8) : (4/8 - 3/8) = 1:1.
4. ALLIGATION ON SPEEDS RETURNS A RATIO OF TIMES, NOT DISTANCES, because average speed is a time-weighted average.
   Worked: 480 km covered partly at 40 km/h and partly at 60 km/h in 10 hours, so the average is 48 km/h. Alligation on 40 and 60 about 48 gives (60-48):(48-40) = 12:8 = 3:2, which is the ratio of TIMES: 6 hours at 40 km/h and 4 hours at 60 km/h. Distances are then 240 km and 240 km.
5. REPLACEMENT FORMULA. From a vessel of volume x containing a pure liquid, remove y and replace with another liquid, n times. Pure liquid remaining = x(1 - y/x)^n.
   Worked: 40 L of milk, 4 L removed and replaced with water, done twice. Milk left = 40 x (1 - 4/40)^2 = 40 x (0.9)^2 = 40 x 0.81 = 32.4 L. Water = 7.6 L. Ratio 32.4 : 7.6 = 81 : 19.
6. THE REPLACEMENT FORMULA APPLIES ONLY WHEN WHAT IS REMOVED IS THE MIXTURE. If the question removes pure milk, or adds water without removing anything, go back to first principles and track the two components separately.
7. ADD-WATER-TO-CHANGE-RATIO PATTERN. The component NOT being added stays constant; anchor on it.
   Worked: 60 L of a 7:3 milk-water mixture. Milk = 42, water = 18. To make it 3:2, milk stays 42, so 42/(18+x) = 3/2 -> 84 = 54 + 3x -> x = 10 L of water. (Check: 42:28 = 3:2.)
8. DISHONEST-DEALER PATTERN. A milkman sells at cost price but gains g% by adding water. Then water : milk = g : 100. For a 25% gain, water:milk = 1:4.
tricks: Alligation is a general weighted-average reverser, not a mixtures-only tool. Use it for 'what ratio of investments at 8% and 12% gives an average return of 9.5%' — (12-9.5):(9.5-8) = 2.5:1.5 = 5:3 — and it lands in 15 seconds where the algebra takes 60.

Always subtract the SMALL value from the mean and the mean from the LARGE value, then cross them. Writing the two differences in the same order they appear in the question is the source of nearly every inverted answer; committing to 'small on the left, always' removes the decision entirely.

For the replacement formula, compute (1 - y/x) once as a fraction and raise it: with x = 40 and y = 4 the factor is 9/10, so after three rounds it is 729/1000 and the milk is 40 x 729/1000 = 29.16 L. Working with 9/10 rather than 0.9 keeps the arithmetic exact and fast.

In add-water and add-milk questions, anchor on the component that does not change and write ONE equation, not two. The unchanging component is stated in the question by omission — if only water is added, milk is your anchor.

Sanity-check the direction of every alligation answer: if the mean is closer to the cheaper value, you need MORE of the cheaper item, so its share of the ratio must be the larger one. This one-second check catches an inverted ratio before you commit to an option.
traps: Inverting the alligation ratio. For c = 30, d = 45, m = 36 the answer is 3:2 in favour of the cheaper rice, because 36 sits closer to 30. Writing 2:3 gives an option that will be present among the five.

Reading the alligation output on speeds as a ratio of distances. It is a ratio of TIMES. In the 480 km example the time ratio is 3:2 while the distance ratio is 1:1 — completely different numbers, and both appear as options.

Applying x(1 - y/x)^n when the question replaced a mixture only once but described it in two sentences, or when the question removed PURE milk rather than the mixture. The formula's derivation assumes the removed portion has the same composition as the vessel.

Computing what remains and reporting it as the answer when the question asked for the quantity of the ADDED liquid, or vice versa. In the 40 L example, 32.4 and 7.6 are both correct numbers for different questions.

Treating a three-way mixture as one alligation. Alligation handles exactly two ingredients at a time. For three, either pair two of them first into a known intermediate mixture, or set up straight algebra.
In the dishonest-dealer pattern, computing water as g% of the TOTAL rather than of the milk. A 25% gain means 25 parts water per 100 parts milk, so water is 1/5 of the final mixture, not 1/4.

q-partnership.whatItIs: Dividing a business profit among people who put in different amounts of money for different lengths of time. The single governing rule is that profit is shared in the ratio of capital multiplied by time — sometimes called the ratio of 'rupee-months'. When everyone invests for the same duration (a 'simple' partnership), the time factor cancels and profit follows the ratio of capitals alone. When durations differ (a 'compound' partnership), you must multiply. A third layer appears when one partner actively manages the business and takes a salary or commission off the top before the remainder is divided. There is no formula beyond capital x time; the difficulty is entirely in reading the timeline correctly.
q-partnership.coreMethod:
1. BUILD A TIMELINE, NOT AN EQUATION. Write each partner on a row and mark the months for which each amount was invested. This is the whole skill.
2. COMPUTE CAPITAL x MONTHS FOR EACH PARTNER, then reduce to the smallest ratio.
   Worked: A invests Rs 12,000 for 12 months, B invests Rs 18,000 for 10 months. A = 144, B = 180 (dropping the common thousands). Ratio 144:180 = 4:5. On a profit of Rs 7,200: one part = 7200/9 = 800, so A gets Rs 3,200 and B gets Rs 4,000.
3. IF A PARTNER CHANGES HIS CAPITAL MID-YEAR, SPLIT HIS ROW INTO SEGMENTS AND ADD.
   Worked: A starts with Rs 20,000. After 6 months he adds Rs 10,000. B joins after 4 months with Rs 30,000. Over 12 months: A = 20,000 x 6 + 30,000 x 6 = 300,000. B = 30,000 x 8 = 240,000. Ratio 300:240 = 5:4. On a profit of Rs 36,000, A gets Rs 20,000 and B gets Rs 16,000.
4. IF SOMEONE WITHDRAWS, SUBTRACT — do not restart the clock. 'A withdraws half his capital after 8 months' means full capital for 8 months plus half capital for 4 months.
5. WORKING PARTNER: DEDUCT THE SALARY OR COMMISSION FIRST, THEN DIVIDE THE REMAINDER by capital x time.
   Worked: A and B invest Rs 40,000 and Rs 60,000 for the whole year. A manages the business and receives 10% of the profit for doing so; the rest is divided in the capital ratio. Total profit Rs 22,000. A's commission = Rs 2,200. Remainder Rs 19,800 splits 2:3, giving A Rs 7,920 and B Rs 11,880. A's total = Rs 10,120.
6. THREE PARTNERS ARE NO HARDER. Compute three products, reduce, divide the profit into the sum of parts.
   Worked: A, B, C invest Rs 5,000 for 12 months, Rs 6,000 for 9 months, Rs 8,000 for 6 months. Products 60,000 : 54,000 : 48,000 = 10:9:8. On a profit of Rs 40,500, one part = 40,500/27 = 1,500, so shares are Rs 15,000, Rs 13,500 and Rs 12,000.
7. IF PROFITS ARE EQUAL, CAPITAL IS INVERSELY PROPORTIONAL TO TIME. Equal shares from investments held for 4 and 6 months means the capitals were in the ratio 6:4 = 3:2.
8. IF THE QUESTION GIVES INVESTMENT RATIO a:b AND TIME RATIO p:q SEPARATELY, the profit ratio is ap:bq in one line — never reconstruct actual rupees.
tricks: Cancel zeros and common factors before multiplying. Rs 24,000 for 8 months versus Rs 36,000 for 10 months becomes 24 x 8 = 192 against 36 x 10 = 360, then 192:360 = 8:15. Multiplying the full rupee figures produces six-digit numbers and costs 20-30 seconds for no gain.

Convert 'a year' into 12 months at the top of the page and work exclusively in months. Mixing 1 year for one partner with 8 months for another is the timeline error that produces most wrong answers here.

When only the ratio is asked, combine the investment ratio and the time ratio by direct multiplication: investments 3:4 held for 5:3 months gives profit ratio 15:12 = 5:4, in a single line and about 10 seconds.

Compute the value of ONE PART first, then multiply out. Total profit divided by the sum of the ratio terms gives one part; every partner's share is then a single multiplication. This also lets you verify instantly, because the shares must add back to the total.

For working-partner questions, write the answer in the form 'commission + share' and answer whichever the question asked. Marking clearly which of the two numbers you have computed prevents the classic error of reporting only the share when the question asked for the total received.
traps: Dividing by capitals alone when the investment periods differ. If A puts in Rs 30,000 for 6 months and B Rs 20,000 for 12 months, the ratio is 180:240 = 3:4 in B's favour, not 3:2 in A's favour. Both numbers will be among the five options.

Splitting the WHOLE profit in the capital ratio and then adding the working partner's commission on top. The commission comes out first; the remainder is what gets divided. Doing it the wrong way round overstates the manager's total.
Confusing 'a commission of 10% of the profit' with '10% of his own share'. These give different answers, and IBPS uses both phrasings.
Restarting the clock when a partner adds capital. Adding Rs 10,000 after 6 months does not mean Rs 30,000 for 12 months; it means Rs 20,000 for 6 months plus Rs 30,000 for 6 months.
Mishandling 'B joined after 4 months'. B's investment period is 8 months, not 4. Reading the stated number as the duration rather than the delay is a specific and very common misreading.

Assuming the profit is split equally when the question mentions that the partners are equal partners in the FIRM. Equality of standing is not equality of capital; only the rupee-month products decide the split unless the question explicitly says profits are shared equally.
q-partnership.timeTarget: Two partners, same period: 20-30 seconds. Two or three partners with different periods: 40-50 seconds. Mid-year addition or withdrawal: 55-70 seconds. Working partner with commission: 60-75 seconds. Question giving investment ratio and time ratio and asking for the profit ratio: 15-20 seconds. Partnership rewards clean bookkeeping more than speed of arithmetic — the timeline should take longer to draw than the sums take to compute.
q-partnership.masteryCheck: You have mastered this when, on reading 'A started a business with Rs 21,000 and after 4 months B joined with Rs 36,000; find the ratio in which the annual profit is divided', you write 21 x 12 = 252 against 36 x 8 = 288, reduce to 7:8, and finish in under 35 seconds. Second check: given a working partner taking 15% of a Rs 40,000 profit as commission with capitals 3:2, produce both his commission (Rs 6,000) and his total (Rs 6,000 + 3/5 x 34,000 = Rs 26,400) without hesitating over the order of operations. Third check: 10 mixed questions, 9 correct, in 9 minutes.
questionPatterns: Different periods: 'A invests Rs 8,000 for 9 months and B invests Rs 6,000 for 12 months. If the profit is Rs 4,800, find B's share.' (72:72 = 1:1 -> Rs 2,400 each.)
Joining late: 'A begins with Rs 45,000; B joins after 3 months with Rs 30,000. Find the ratio in which the annual profit is shared.' (45 x 12 = 540 against 30 x 9 = 270 -> 2:1.)

Mid-year change: 'A invests Rs 10,000. After 6 months he withdraws Rs 4,000. B invests Rs 8,000 throughout. Find the profit-sharing ratio for the year.' (A = 10 x 6 + 6 x 6 = 96; B = 8 x 12 = 96 -> 1:1.)

Working partner: 'A and B invest Rs 25,000 and Rs 35,000. A, being the working partner, takes 20% of the profit as remuneration and the remainder is split in the capital ratio. If the total profit is Rs 30,000, find A's total receipt.' (Commission Rs 6,000; remainder Rs 24,000 split 5:7 -> A gets Rs 10,000; total Rs 16,000.)
Three partners: 'A, B and C invest in the ratio 2:3:4 for periods in the ratio 4:3:2. Find the profit-sharing ratio.' (8:9:8.)

Reverse question: 'In a partnership A's share of a Rs 21,000 profit is Rs 6,000. If B invested Rs 45,000 for the full year and A invested for 8 months, find A's capital.' (A:B = 6,000:15,000 = 2:5; A's capital x 8 : 45,000 x 12 = 2:5 -> A's capital x 8 = 216,000 -> Rs 27,000.)

q-partnership.aiPrompt: Act as an IBPS Clerk 2026 quant coach. Give me 12 Partnership questions in IBPS Clerk style, each with EXACTLY FIVE options labelled (a) to (e). Compute every answer yourself before writing the options and discard any question whose shares are not whole rupees. In each question include one distractor produced by ignoring the time factor and one produced by mistaking a 'joined after n months' delay for a duration of n months. Provide an answer key showing the rupee-month products explicitly, name the trap behind each distractor, and give a target time in seconds. Do not offer any answer-guessing pattern.
q-partnership.blockPlan: An 80-minute block; Partnership is small enough to finish in one sitting. Minutes 0-10: write the rule 'profit ratio = capital x months' and the four timeline situations (joins late, withdraws, adds, working partner) as four blank row-diagrams. Minutes 10-30: 12 straightforward different-period questions with the discipline of drawing the timeline before computing — no mental shortcuts yet. Minutes 30-50: 10 mid-year change questions; for each, check that the segments of one partner's row add up to 12 months before multiplying. Minutes 50-70: 8 working-partner questions, alternating percentage commission and fixed salary, writing 'commission =' and 'share =' as separate labelled lines every time. Minutes 70-80: 5 ratio-only questions solved in one line each (ap:bq), timed at 20 seconds. Review for 20 minutes a week later; this topic decays slowly once the timeline habit is formed.
q-partnership.weightageNote: Partnership is a regular member of the IBPS Clerk arithmetic rotation, generally worth about 1 question in Prelims and 1 in Mains. It is worth studying early because it is closed, short and almost entirely procedural: there is one rule and four timeline situations, so a single focused block gets most aspirants to near-certainty. It also shares its ratio machinery with Averages, Ratio & Proportion and Time & Work, so the practice transfers.
